entries.fe2e413abfc8583b4966a07ee2ce0eb24b6906df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv79"/><title type="x-s3">Proper Treatment of Fools.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv79"/> <div sID="gen14471" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool. <div eID="gen14471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is too common a thing for honour to be given to fools, who are utterly unworthy of it and unfit for it. Bad men, who have neither wit nor grace, are sometimes preferred by princes, and applauded and cried up by the people. <hi type="italic">Folly is set in great dignity,</hi> as Solomon observed, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">Eccl. x. 6</reference>. 2. It is very absurd and unbecoming when it is so. It is an incongruous <hi type="italic">as snow in summer,</hi> and as great a disorder in the commonwealth as that is in the course of nature and in the seasons of the year; nay, it is as injurious <hi type="italic">as rain in harvest,</hi> which hinders the labourers and spoils the fruits of the earth when they are ready to be gathered. When bad men are in power they commonly abuse their power, in discouraging virtue, and giving countenance to wickedness, for want of wisdom to discern it and grace to detest it.
entries.ac48c44d7594fa60316c5fca8756e7272990615c: <div eID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come. <div eID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14474" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The folly of passion. It makes men scatter <hi type="italic">causeless curses,</hi> wishing ill to others upon presumption that they are bad and have done ill, when either they mistake the person or misunderstand the fact, or they call evil good and good evil. Give honour to a fool, and he thunders out his anathemas against all that he is disgusted with, right or wrong. Great men, when wicked, think they have a privilege to keep those about them in awe, by cursing them, and swearing at them, which yet is an expression of the most impotent malice and shows their weakness as much as their wickedness. 2. The safety of innocency. He that is cursed without cause, whether by furious imprecations or solemn anathemas, the curse shall do him no more harm than the bird that flies over his head, than Goliath's curses did to David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.43">1 Sam. xvii. 43</reference>. It will fly away like the sparrow or the wild dove, which go nobody knows where, till they return to their proper place, as the curse will at length return upon the head of him that uttered it.
entries.e588545104dbfae7beacc0d82a2449dd144dfe05: <div eID="gen14474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14475" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back. <div eID="gen14475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14476" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. Wicked men are compared to <hi type="italic">the horse</hi> and <hi type="italic">the ass,</hi> so brutish are they, so unreasonable, so unruly, and not to be governed but by force or fear, so low has sin sunk men, so much below themselves. Man indeed is <hi type="italic">born like the wild ass's colt,</hi> but as some by the grace of God are changed, and become rational, so others by custom in sin are hardened, and become more and more sottish, <hi type="italic">as the horse and the mule,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Ps. xxxii. 9</reference>. 2. Direction is given to use them accordingly. Princes, instead of giving <hi type="italic">honour to a fool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">v. 1</reference>), must put disgrace upon him—instead of putting power into his hand, must exercise power over him. A <hi type="italic">horse</hi> unbroken needs <hi type="italic">a whip</hi> for correction, and an <hi type="italic">ass a bridle</hi> for direction and to check him when he would turn out of the way; so a vicious man, who will not be under the guidance and restraint of religion and reason, ought to be whipped and bridled, to be rebuked severely, and made to smart for what he has done amiss, and to be restrained from offending any more.
entries.b20f14134f7c4a30d1f9a26b845ac7d2b5472da3: <div eID="gen14476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14477" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him. <hi type="super">5</hi> Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit. <div eID="gen14477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14478" type="x-p"/> See here the noble security of the scripture-style, which seems to contradict itself, but really does not. Wise men have need to be directed how to deal with fools; and they have never more need of wisdom than in dealing with such, to know when to keep silence and when to speak, for there may be a time for both. 1. In some cases a wise man will not set his wit to that of a fool so far as to <hi type="italic">answer him according to his folly</hi> "If he boast of himself, do not answer him by boasting of thyself. If he rail and talk passionately, do not thou rail and talk passionately too. If he tell one great lie, do not thou tell another to match it. If he calumniate thy friends, do not thou calumniate his. If he banter, do not answer him in his own language, <hi type="italic">lest thou be like him,</hi> even thou, who knowest better things, who hast more sense, and hast been better taught." 2. Yet, in other cases, a wise man will use his wisdom for the conviction of a fool, when, by taking notice of what he says, there may be hopes of doing good, or at least preventing further, mischief, either to himself or others. "If thou have reason to think that thy silence will be deemed an evidence of the weakness of thy cause, or of thy own weakness, in such a case <hi type="italic">answer him,</hi> and let it be an answer <hi type="italic">ad hominem—to the man,</hi> beat him at his own weapons, and that will be an answer <hi type="italic">ad rem—to the point,</hi> or as good as one. If he offer any thing that looks like an argument, an answer that, and suit thy answer to his case. If he think, because thou dost not answer him, that what he says is unanswerable, then give him an answer, <hi type="italic">lest he be wise in his own conceit</hi> and boast of a victory." For (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.35">Luke vii. 35</reference>) Wisdom's children must justify her.
entries.f0a5ef849947ea4155457d992ff553ada3ee8c78: <div eID="gen14478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, <hi type="italic">and</hi> drinketh damage. <hi type="super">7</hi> The legs of the lame are not equal: so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a parable in the mouth of fools. <hi type="super">8</hi> As he that bindeth a stone in a sling, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that giveth honour to a fool. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a parable in the mouth of fools. <div eID="gen14479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14480" type="x-p"/> To recommend wisdom to us, and to quicken us to the diligent use of all the means for the getting of wisdom, Solomon here shows that fools are fit for nothing; they are either sottish men, who will never think and design at all, or vicious men, who will never think and design well. 1. They are not fit to be entrusted with any business, not fit to go on an errand (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that</hi> does but <hi type="italic">send a message by the hand of a fool,</hi> of a careless heedless person, one who is so full of his jests and so given to his pleasures that he cannot apply his mind to any thing that is serious, will find his message misunderstood, the one half of it forgotten, the rest awkwardly delivered, and so many blunders made about it that he might as well have <hi type="italic">cut off his legs,</hi> that is, never have sent him. Nay, he will <hi type="italic">drink damage;</hi> it will be very much to his prejudice to have employed such a one, who, instead of bringing him a good account of his affairs, will abuse him and put a trick upon him; for, in Solomon's language, a knave and a fool are of the same signification. It will turn much to a man's disgrace to make use of the service of a fool, for people will be apt to judge of the master by his messenger. 2. They are not fit to have any honour put upon them. He had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Honour is not seemly for a fool;</hi> here he shows that it is lost and thrown away upon him, as if a man should throw a precious stone, or a stone fit to be used in weighing, into a heap of common stones, where it would be buried and of no use; it is as absurd as if a man should <hi type="italic">dress up a stone in purple</hi> (so others); nay, it is dangerous, it is like <hi type="italic">a stone bound in a sling,</hi> with which a man will be likely to do hurt. To <hi type="italic">give honour to a fool</hi> is to put a sword in a madman's hand, with which we know not what mischief he may do, even to those that put it into his hand. 3. They are not fit to deliver wise sayings, nor should they undertake to handle any matter of weight, though they should be instructed concerning it, and be able to say something to it. Wise sayings, as a foolish man delivers them and applies them (in such a manner that one may know he does not rightly understand them), lose their excellency and usefulness: <hi type="italic">A parable in the mouth of fools</hi> ceases to be a parable, and becomes a jest. If a man who lives a wicked life, yet speaks religiously and takes God's covenant into his mouth, (1.) He does but shame himself and his profession: As <hi type="italic">the legs of the lame are not equal,</hi> by reason of which their going is unseemly, so unseemly is it for a fool to pretend to speak apophthegms, and give advice, and for a man to talk devoutly whose conversation is a constant contradiction to his talk and gives him the lie. His good words raise him up, but then his bad life takes him down, and so his <hi type="italic">legs are not equal.</hi> "A wise saying," (says bishop Patrick) "doth as ill become a fool as dancing doth a cripple; for, as his lameness never so much appears as when he would seem nimble, so the other's folly is never so ridiculous as when he would seem wise." As therefore it is best for a lame man to keep his seat, so it is best for a silly man, or a bad man, to hold his tongue. (2.) He does but do mischief with it to himself and others, as a drunkard does with a thorn, or any other sharp thing which he takes in his hand, with which he tears himself and those about him, because he knows not how to manage it. Those that talk well and do not live well, their good words will aggravate their own condemnation and others will be hardened by their inconsistency with themselves. Some give this sense of it: The sharpest saying, by which a sinner, one would think, should be pricked to the heart, makes no more impression upon a fool, no, though it come out of his own mouth, than the scratch of a thorn does upon the hand of a man when he is drunk, who then feels it not nor complains of it, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.35">ch. xxiii. 35</reference>.  <div eID="gen14480" type="x-p"/>
entries.720592c0704cd28960e7afda498ee87ae71db5ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv80"/><title type="x-s3">The Conduct of Fools.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv80"/> <div sID="gen14481" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The great <hi type="italic">God</hi> that formed all <hi type="italic">things</hi> both rewardeth the fool, and rewardeth transgressors. <div eID="gen14481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14482" type="x-p"/> Our translation gives this verse a different reading in the text and in the margin; and accordingly it expresses either, 1. The equity of a good God. The <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> (so <hi type="italic">Rab</hi> signifies), or, as we read it, <hi type="italic">The great God that formed all things</hi> at first, and still governs them in infinite wisdom, renders to every man according to his work. He <hi type="italic">rewards the fool,</hi> who sinned through ignorance, <hi type="italic">who knew not his Lord's will, with few stripes;</hi> and he <hi type="italic">rewards the transgressor,</hi> who sinned presumptuously and with a high hand, who <hi type="italic">knew his Lord's will and would not do it, with many stripes.</hi> Some understand it of the goodness of God's common providence even to fools and transgressors, on whom <hi type="italic">he causes his sun to shine</hi> and <hi type="italic">his rain to fall.</hi> Or, 2. The iniquity of a bad prince (so the margin reads it): <hi type="italic">A great man grieves all, and he hires the fool; he hires also the transgressors.</hi> When a wicked man gets power in his hand, by himself, and by the fools and knaves whom he employs under him, whom he hires and chooses to make use of, he grieves all who are under him and is vexatious to them. We should therefore <hi type="italic">pray for kings and all in authority,</hi> that, under them, our lives may be quiet and peaceable.
entries.4c651f85bf8e0f7008181684c073ca43215f9559: <div eID="gen14482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14483" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> As a dog returneth to his vomit, <hi type="italic">so</hi> a fool returneth to his folly. <div eID="gen14483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14484" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What an abominable thing sin is, and how hateful sometimes it is made to appear, even to the sinner himself. When his conscience is convinced, or he feels smart from his sin, he is sick of it, and vomits it up; he seems then to detest it and to be willing to part with it. It is in itself, and, first or last, will be to the sinner, more loathsome than the vomit of a dog, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.2">Ps. xxxvi. 2</reference>. 2. How apt sinners are to relapse into it notwithstanding. As the dog, after he has gained ease by vomiting that which burdened his stomach, yet goes and licks it up again, so sinners, who have been convinced only and not converted, return to sin again, forgetting how sick it made them. The apostle (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.22">2 Pet. ii. 22</reference>) applies this proverb to those that <hi type="italic">have known the way of righteousness</hi> but are <hi type="italic">turned from it;</hi> but God will <hi type="italic">spue them out of his mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.16">Rev. iii. 16</reference>.
entries.2f41124876536203c9cf27bf46d529ef4e093267: <div eID="gen14484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14485" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? <hi type="italic">there is</hi> more hope of a fool than of him. <div eID="gen14485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14486" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A spiritual disease supposed, and that is self-conceit: <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man?</hi> Yes, we see many a one, <hi type="italic">wise in his own conceit,</hi> who has some little sense, but is proud of it, thinks it much more than it is, more than any of his neighbours, have, and enough, so that he needs no more, has such a conceit of his own abilities as makes him opinionative, dogmatical, and censorious; and all the use he makes of his knowledge is that it puffs him up. Or, if by a wise man we understand a religious man, it describes the character of those who, making some show of religion, conclude their spiritual state to be good when really it is very bad, like Laodicea, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Rev. iii. 17</reference>. 2. The danger of this disease. It is in a manner desperate: <hi type="italic">There is more hope of a fool,</hi> that knows and owns himself to be such, <hi type="italic">than of</hi> such a one. Solomon was not only a wise man himself, but a teacher of wisdom; and this observation he made upon his pupils, that he found his work most difficult and least successful with those that had a good opinion of themselves and were not sensible that they needed instruction. Therefore he that <hi type="italic">seems</hi> to himself <hi type="italic">to be wise</hi> must <hi type="italic">become a fool, that he may be wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">1 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. There is more hope of a publican than of a proud Pharisee, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.32">Matt. xxi. 32</reference>. Many are hindered from being truly wise and religious by a false and groundless conceit that they are so, <reference osisRef="John.9.40-John.9.41">John ix. 40, 41</reference>.  <div eID="gen14486" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fac500e4fef1068bc1b55ed4f69211a7404944b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv81"/><title type="x-s3">The Disgrace of Slothfulness.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv81"/> <div sID="gen14487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> The slothful <hi type="italic">man</hi> saith, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a lion in the way; a lion <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the streets. <div eID="gen14487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14488" type="x-p"/> When a man talks foolishly we say, He talks idly; for none betray their folly more than those who are idle and go about to excuse themselves in their idleness. As men's folly makes them slothful, so their slothfulness makes them foolish. Observe, 1. What <hi type="italic">the slothful man</hi> really dreads. He dreads <hi type="italic">the way, the streets,</hi> the place where work is to be done and a journey to be gone; he hates business, hates every thing that requires care and labour. 2. What he dreams of, and pretends to dread—<hi type="italic">a lion in the way.</hi> When he is pressed to be diligent, either in his worldly affairs or in the business of religion, this is his excuse (and a sorry excuse it is, as bad as none), <hi type="italic">There is a lion in the way,</hi> some insuperable difficulty or danger which he cannot pretend to grapple with. Lions frequent woods and deserts; and, in the day-time, when man has business to do, they are in their dens, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.22-Ps.104.23">Ps. civ. 22, 23</reference>. But the sluggard fancies, or rather pretends to fancy, <hi type="italic">a lion in the streets,</hi> whereas the lion is only in his own fancy, nor is he so fierce as he is painted. Note, It is a foolish thing to frighten ourselves from real duties by fancied difficulties, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Eccl. xi. 4</reference>.
entries.a96387635796f8fa791b296990feb747625bf166: <div eID="gen14488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14489" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> the door turneth upon his hinges, so <hi type="italic">doth</hi> the slothful upon his bed. <div eID="gen14489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14490" type="x-p"/> Having seen the slothful man in fear of his work, here we find him in love with his ease; he lies in his bed on one side till he is weary of that, and then turns to the other, but still in his bed, when it is far in the day and work is to be done, as the door is moved, but not removed; and so his business is neglected and his opportunities are let slip. See the sluggard's character. 1. He is one that does not care to get out of his bed, but seems to be hung upon it, <hi type="italic">as the door upon the hinges.</hi> Bodily ease, too much consulted, is the sad occasion of many a spiritual disease. Those that love sleep will prove in the end to have loved death. 2. He does not care to get forward with his business; in that he stirs to and fro a little, but to no purpose; he is where he was. Slothful professors turn, in profession, like <hi type="italic">the door upon the hinges.</hi> The world and the flesh are the two hinges on which they are hung, and though they move in a course of external services, have got into road of duties, and tread around in them like the horse in the mill, yet they get no good, they get no ground, they are never the nearer heaven—sinners unchanged, saints unimproved.
entries.3d2ac9d5e2bc4f3b18bdd8b599f035ead8e0fdc4: <div eID="gen14490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14491" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The slothful hideth his hand in <hi type="italic">his</hi> bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth. <div eID="gen14491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14492" type="x-p"/> The sluggard has now, with much ado, got out of his bed, but he might as well have lain there still for any thing he is likely to bring to pass in his work, so awkwardly does he go about it. Observe, 1. The pretence he makes for his slothfulness: He <hi type="italic">hides his hand in his bosom</hi> for fear of cold; next to his warm bed in his warm bosom. Or he pretends that he is lame, as some do that make a trade of begging; something ails his hand; he would have it thought that it is blistered with yesterday's hard work. Or it intimates, in general, his aversion to business; he has tried, and his hands are not used to labour, and therefore he hugs himself in his own ease and cares for nobody. Note, It is common for those that will not do their duty to pretend they cannot. <hi type="italic">I cannot dig,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.3">Luke xvi. 3</reference>. 2. The prejudice he sustains by his slothfulness. He himself is the loser by it, for he starves himself: <hi type="italic">It grieves him to bring his hand to his mouth,</hi> that is, he cannot find in his heart to feed himself, but dreads, as if it were a mighty toil, to lift his hand to his head. It is an elegant hyperbole, aggravating his sin, that he cannot endure to take the least pains, no, not for the greatest profit, and showing how his sin is his punishment. Those that are slothful in the business of religion will not be at the pains to feed their own souls with the word of God, the bread of life, nor to fetch in promised blessings by prayer, though they might have them for the fetching.
entries.c1fcf9eca826bcd8632e8529cecea5e1f8472c7c: <div eID="gen14492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14493" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> The sluggard <hi type="italic">is</hi> wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason. <div eID="gen14493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14494" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The high opinion which the sluggard has of himself, notwithstanding the gross absurdity and folly of his slothfulness: He thinks himself <hi type="italic">wiser than seven men,</hi> than seven wise men, for they are such as <hi type="italic">can render a reason.</hi> It is the wisdom of a man to be able to <hi type="italic">render a reason,</hi> of a good man to be able to give <hi type="italic">a reason of the hope that is in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>. What we do we should be able to <hi type="italic">render a reason</hi> for, though perhaps we may not have wit enough to show the fallacy of every objection against it. He that takes pains in religion can render a good reason for it; he knows that he is working for a good Master and that <hi type="italic">his labour shall not be in vain.</hi> But <hi type="italic">the sluggard</hi> thinks himself <hi type="italic">wiser than seven</hi> such; for let seven such persuade him to be diligent, with all the reasons they can render for it, it is to no purpose; his own determination, he thinks, answer enough to them and all their reasons. 2. The reference that this has to his slothfulness. It is <hi type="italic">the sluggard,</hi> above all men, that is thus self-conceited; for, (1.) His good opinion of himself is the cause of his slothfulness; he will not take pains to get wisdom because he thinks he is wise enough already. A conceit of the sufficiency of our attainments is a great enemy to our improvement. (2.) His slothfulness is the cause of his good opinion of himself. If he would but take pains to examine himself, and compare himself with the laws of wisdom, he would have other thoughts of himself. Indulged slothfulness is at the bottom of prevailing self-conceitedness. Nay, (3.) So wretchedly besotted is he that he takes his slothfulness to be his wisdom; he thinks it is his wisdom to make much of himself, and take all the ease he can get, and do no more in religion than he needs must, to avoid suffering, to sit still and see what other people do, that he may have the pleasure of finding fault with them. Of such sluggards, who are proud of that which is their shame, their is little hope, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">v. 12</reference>.  <div eID="gen14494" type="x-p"/>
entries.348a0ebfaab76689f15465295ee30a7c3858bd94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv82"/><title type="x-s3">Hatred and Strife.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv82"/> <div sID="gen14495" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> He that passeth by, <hi type="italic">and</hi> meddleth with strife <hi type="italic">belonging</hi> not to him, <hi type="italic">is like</hi> one that taketh a dog by the ears. <div eID="gen14495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14496" type="x-p"/> 1. That which is here condemned is <hi type="italic">meddling with strife that belongs not to us.</hi> If we must not be hasty to strive in our own cause (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.8">ch. xxv. 8</reference>), much less in other people's, especially theirs that we are no way related to or concerned in, but light on accidentally as we pass by. If we can be instrumental to make peace between those that are at variance we must do it, though we should thereby get the ill-will of both sides, at least while they are in their heat; but to make ourselves busy in other men's matters, and parties in other men's quarrels, is not only to court our own trouble, but to thrust ourselves into temptation. <hi type="italic">Who made</hi> me <hi type="italic">a judge?</hi> Let them end it, as they began it, between themselves. 2. We are cautioned against it because of the danger it exposes us to; it is like taking a snarling cur <hi type="italic">by the ears,</hi> that will snap at you and bite you; you had better have let him alone, for you cannot get clear of him when you would, and must thank yourselves if you come off with a wound and dishonour. He that has got <hi type="italic">a dog by the ears,</hi> if he lets him go he flies at him, if he keeps his hold, he has his hands full, and can do nothing else. Let every one <hi type="italic">with quietness work and mind his own business,</hi> and not with unquietness quarrel and meddle with other people's business.
entries.50f7c04a9bfbd1fa7a5c6d0be12f540b035282a1: <div eID="gen14496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14497" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> As a mad <hi type="italic">man</hi> who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, <hi type="super">19</hi> So <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport? <div eID="gen14497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14498" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How mischievous those are that make no scruple of <hi type="italic">deceiving their neighbours;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">as madmen that cast firebrands, arrows, and death,</hi> so much hurt may they do by their deceits. They value themselves upon it as polite cunning men, but really they are <hi type="italic">as madmen.</hi> There is not a greater madness in the world than a wilful sin. It is not only the passionate furious man, but the malicious deceitful man, that is <hi type="italic">a madman;</hi> he does in effect <hi type="italic">cast fire-brands, arrows, and death;</hi> he does more mischief than he can imagine. Fraud and falsehood burn like fire-brands, kill, even at a distance, like arrows. 2. See how frivolous the excuse is which men commonly make for the mischief they do, that they did it in a jest; with this they think to turn it off when they are reproved for it, <hi type="italic">Am not I in sport?</hi> But it will prove dangerous playing with fire and jesting with edge-tools. Not that those are to be commended who are captious, and can take no jest (those that themselves are <hi type="italic">wise must suffer fools,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.19-2Cor.11.20">2 Cor. xi. 19, 20</reference>), but those are certainly to be condemned who are any way abusive to their neighbours, impose upon their credulity, cheat them in their bargains with them, tell lies to them or tell lies of them, give them ill language, or sully their reputation, and then think to excuse it by saying that they did but jest. <hi type="italic">Am not I in sport?</hi> He that sins in just must repent in earnest, or his sin will be his ruin. Truth is too valuable a thing to be sold for a jest, and so is the reputation of our neighbour. By lying and slandering in jest men learn themselves, and teach others, to lie and slander in earnest; and a false report, raised in mirth, may be spread in malice; besides, if a man may tell a lie to make himself merry, why not to make himself rich, and so <hi type="italic">truth quite perishes,</hi> and men <hi type="italic">teach their tongues to tell lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.9.5">Jer. ix. 5</reference>. If men would consider that a lie comes from the devil, and brings to hell-fire, surely that would spoil the sport of it; it is <hi type="italic">casting arrows and death</hi> to themselves.
entries.766fc213f3222f91b41d98b7dc942829cd021a9a: <div eID="gen14498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14499" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Where no wood is, <hi type="italic">there</hi> the fire goeth out: so where <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no talebearer, the strife ceaseth. 21 <hi type="italic">As</hi> coals <hi type="italic">are</hi> to burning coals, and wood to fire; so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a contentious man to kindle strife. <hi type="super">22</hi> The words of a talebearer <hi type="italic">are</hi> as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly. <div eID="gen14499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14500" type="x-p"/> Contention is as a fire; it heats the spirit, burns up all that is good, and puts families and societies into a flame. Now here we are told how that fire is commonly kindled and kept burning, that we may avoid the occasions of strife and so prevent the mischievous consequences of it. If then we would keep the peace, 1. We must not give ear to <hi type="italic">talebearers,</hi> for they feed the fire of contention with fuel; nay, they spread it with combustible matter; the tales they carry are fireballs. Those who by insinuating base characters, revealing secrets, and misrepresenting words and actions, do what they can to make relations, friends, and neighbours, jealous one of another, to alienate them one from another, and sow discord among them, are to be banished out of families and all societies, and then strife will as surely cease as the fire will go out when it has no fuel; the contenders will better understand one another and come to a better temper; old stories will soon be forgotten when there are no new ones told to keep up the remembrance of them, and both sides will see how they have been imposed upon by a common enemy. Whisperers and backbiters are incendiaries not to be suffered. To illustrate this, he repeats (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.22">v. 22</reference>) what he had said before (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.8">ch. xviii. 8</reference>), that <hi type="italic">the words of a tale-bearer are as wounds,</hi> deep and dangerous wounds, wounds in the vitals. They wound the reputation of him who is belied, and perhaps the wound proves incurable, and even the plaster of a recantation (which yet can seldom be obtained) may not prove wide enough for it. They wound the love and charity which he to whom they are spoken ought to have for his neighbour and give a fatal stab to friendship and Christian fellowship. We must therefore not only not be tale-bearers ourselves at any time, nor ever do any ill offices, but we should not give the least countenance to those that are. 2. We must not associate with peevish passionate people, that are exceptions, and apt to put the worst constructions upon everything, that pick quarrels upon the least occasion, and are quick, and high, and hot, in resenting affronts. These are <hi type="italic">contentious men,</hi> that <hi type="italic">kindle strife,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.21">v. 21</reference>. The less we have to do with such the better, for it will be very difficult to avoid quarrelling with those that are quarrelsome.
entries.54abb186ccd17e7e8a6b5ba05c265f5fe18684d6: <div eID="gen14500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14501" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Burning lips and a wicked heart <hi type="italic">are like</hi> a potsherd covered with silver dross. <div eID="gen14501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14502" type="x-p"/> This may be meant either, 1. Of <hi type="italic">a wicked heart</hi> showing itself in <hi type="italic">burning lips,</hi> furious, passionate, outrageous words, burning in malice, and persecuting those to whom, or of whom, they are spoken; ill words and ill-will agree as well together as <hi type="italic">a potsherd</hi> and the <hi type="italic">dross of silver,</hi> which, now that the pot is broken and the dross separated from the silver, are fit to be thrown together to the dunghill. 2. Or of <hi type="italic">a wicked heart</hi> disguising itself with <hi type="italic">burning lips,</hi> burning with the professions of love and friendship, and even persecuting a man with flatteries; this is <hi type="italic">like a potsherd covered with</hi> the scum or <hi type="italic">dross of silver,</hi> with which one that is weak may be imposed upon, as if it were of some value, but a wise man is soon aware of the cheat. This sense agrees with the following verses.
entries.1ff72cf98deec80f86a2c7462a71e74451177ef5: <div eID="gen14502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14503" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him; <hi type="super">25</hi> When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for <hi type="italic">there are</hi> seven abominations in his heart. <hi type="super">26</hi> <hi type="italic">Whose</hi> hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the <hi type="italic">whole</hi> congregation. <div eID="gen14503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14504" type="x-p"/> There is cause to complain, not only of the want of sincerity in men's profession of friendship, and that they do not love so well as they pretend nor will serve their friends so much as they promise, but, which is much worse, of wicked designs in the profession of friendship, and the making of it subservient to the most malicious intentions. This is here spoken of as a common thing (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that hates</hi> his neighbour, and is contriving to do him a mischief, yet <hi type="italic">dissembles with his lips,</hi> professes to have a respect for him and to be ready to serve him, talks kindly with him, as Cain with Abel, asks, <hi type="italic">Art thou in health, my brother?</hi> as Joab to Amasa, that his malice may not be suspected and guarded against, and so he may have the fairer opportunity to execute the purposes of it, this man <hi type="italic">lays up deceit within him,</hi> that is, he keeps in his mind the mischief he intends to do his neighbour till he catches him at an advantage. This is malice which has no less of the subtlety than it has of the venom of the old serpent in it. Now, as to this matter, we are here cautioned, 1. Not to be so foolish as to suffer ourselves to be imposed upon by the pretensions of friendship. Remember to distrust when a man <hi type="italic">speaks fair;</hi> be not too forward to <hi type="italic">believe him</hi> unless you know him well, for it is possible there may be <hi type="italic">seven abominations in his heart,</hi> a great many projects of mischief against you, which he is labouring so industriously to conceal with his fair speech. Satan is an enemy that hates us, and yet in his temptations speaks fair, as he did to Eve, but it is madness to give credit to him, <hi type="italic">for there are seven abominations in his heart; seven other spirits</hi> does one unclean spirit bring <hi type="italic">more wicked than himself.</hi> 2. Not to be so wicked as to impose upon any with a profession of friendship; for, though the fraud may be carried on plausibly awhile, it will be brought to light, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.26">v. 26</reference>. He <hi type="italic">whose hatred is covered by deceit</hi> will one time or other be discovered, and <hi type="italic">his wickedness shown,</hi> to his shame and confusion, <hi type="italic">before the whole congregation;</hi> and nothing will do more to make a man odious to all companies. Love (says one) is the best armour, but the worst cloak, and will serve dissemblers as the disguise which Ahab put on and perished in.
entries.5a6cbbc9acfc4cacc557d427b2364f0807f74fc9: <div eID="gen14504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14505" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him. <div eID="gen14505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14506" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What pains men take to do mischief to others. As they put a force upon themselves by concealing their design with a profession of friendship, so they put themselves to a great deal of labour to bring it about; it is <hi type="italic">digging a pit,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">rolling a stone,</hi> hard work, and yet men will not stick at it to gratify their passion and revenge. 2. What preparation they hereby make of mischief to themselves. Their violent dealing will return upon their own heads; they shall themselves <hi type="italic">fall into the pit they digged,</hi> and the stone they rolled <hi type="italic">will return upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15-Ps.7.16">Ps. vii. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.15-Ps.9.16">ix. 15, 16</reference>. The righteous God will take the wise, not only <hi type="italic">in their own craftiness,</hi> but in their own cruelty. It is the plotter's doom. Haman is hanged on a gallows of his own preparing. <div eID="gen14506" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen14507"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14508"/>—————nec lex est justior ulla<l eID="gen14508" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14509"/>Quam necis artifices arte perire sua—<l eID="gen14509" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14510"/>Nor is there any law more just than that the contrivers<l eID="gen14510" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14511"/>of destruction should perish by their own arts.
entries.b7914dd31cd9323f7d68cda01d2d9149d5b7aa2b: <l eID="gen14511" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14507"/> <div sID="gen14512" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> A lying tongue hateth <hi type="italic">those that are</hi> afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin. <div eID="gen14512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14513" type="x-p"/> There are two sorts of lies equally detestable:—1. A slandering lie, which avowedly hates those it is spoken of: <hi type="italic">A lying tongue hates those that are afflicted by it;</hi> it afflicts them by calumnies and reproaches because it hates them, and can thus smite them secretly where they are without defence; and it hates them because it has afflicted them and made them its enemies. The mischief of this is open and obvious; it afflicts, it hates, and owns it, and every body sees it. 2. A flattering lie, which secretly works the ruin of those it is spoken to. In the former the mischief is plain, and men guard against it as well as they can, but in this it is little suspected, and men betray themselves by being credulous of their own praises and the compliments that are passed upon them. A wise man therefore will be more afraid of a flatterer that kisses and kills than of a slanderer that proclaims war.  <chapter eID="Prov.26"/> <div eID="gen14513" type="x-p"/>

entries.976a978a820a1bbf4f7a5cb33c6618dcf45814ec: <div eID="gen24819" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24820" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24821" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24821" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24820" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24822" type="x-p"/> Honor is not seemly in a fool. The correction and treatment suitable to such. Of the slothful man. Of him who interferes with matters which do not concern him. Contentions to be avoided. Of the dissembler and the lying tongue. <div eID="gen24822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24823" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24824" type="x-p"/> As snow in summer - None of these is suitable to the time; and at this unsuitable time, both are unwelcome: so a fool to be in honor is unbecoming.
entries.5d567d7d00144d77ed5d9a0ff39fd17a1ece10ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24825" type="x-p"/> As the bird - צפור tsippor is taken often for the sparrow; but means generally any small bird. As the sparrow flies about the house, and the swallow emigrates to strange countries; so an undeserved malediction may flutter about the neighborhood for a season: but in a short time it will disappear as the bird of passage; and never take effect on the innocent person against whom it was pronounced.
entries.18244c700b5cd346d8f1c84cd683acd4608df7e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24826" type="x-p"/> A whip for the horse - Correction is as suitable to a fool, as a whip is for a horse, or a bridle for an ass.
entries.d0c8731d647a40d72c8dd0508109e91e8108c796: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24827" type="x-p"/> Answer not a fool - On this and the following verse Bishop Warburton, who has written well on many things, and very indifferently on the doctrine of grace, has written with force and perspicuity: "Had this advice been given simply, and without circumstance, to answer the fool, and not to answer him, one who had reverence for the text would satisfy himself in supposing that the different directions referred to the doing a thing in and out of season; <div eID="gen24827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24828" type="x-p"/> 1. The reasons given why a fool should not be answered according to his folly, is, "lest he (the answerer) should be like unto him." <div eID="gen24828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24829" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason given why the fool should be answered according to his folly, is, "lest he (the fool) should be wise in his own conceit." <div eID="gen24829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24830" type="x-p"/> 1. "The cause assigned for forbidding to answer, therefore, plainly insinuates that the defender of religion should not imitate the insulter of it in his modes of disputation, which may be comprised in sophistry, buffoonery, and scurrility. <div eID="gen24830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24831" type="x-p"/> 2. "The cause assigned for directing to answer, as plainly intimates that the sage should address himself to confute the fool upon his own false principles, by showing that they lead to conclusions very wide from, very opposite to, those impieties he would deduce from them. If any thing can allay the fool's vanity, and prevent his being wise in his own conceit, it must be the dishonor of having his own principles turned against himself, and shown to be destructive of his own conclusions." - Treatise on Grace. Preface.
entries.71d53b93bbeafb01d39aecaa3b7be952f6c3f363: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24832" type="x-p"/> Cutteth off the feet - Sending by such a person is utterly useless. My old MS. Bible translates well: Halt in feet and drinking wickednesse that sendith wordis bi a foole messager. Nothing but lameness in himself can vindicate his sending it by such hands; and, after all, the expedient will be worse than the total omission, for he is likely to drink wickedness, i.e., the mischief occasioned by the fool's misconduct. Coverdale nearly hits the sense as usual: "He is lame of his fete, yee dronken is he in vanite, that committeth eny thinge to a foole."
entries.91afd7cbddf65ff267a39fb1bd05811fab266679: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24833" type="x-p"/> As he that bindeth a stone in a sling, so is he that giveth honor to a fool - It is entirely thrown away. This, however, is a difficult proverb; and the versions give but little light on the subject. The Hebrew may be translated, "As a piece of precious stone among a heap of stones, so is he that giveth honor to a fool." Or, As he that putteth a precious stone in a heap of stones. See Parkhurst: but on this interpretation the meaning would rather be, "It is as useless to throw a jewel among a heap of stones to increase its bulk, as to give honor to a fool." <div eID="gen24833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24834" type="x-p"/> As he that sendith a stoon into a hepe of monee; so he that geveth to an unwiisman wirschip - Old MS. Bible. "He that setteth a foole in hye dignite, that is even as yf a man dyd caste a precious stone upon the galous." - Coverdale. This translator refers to the custom of throwing a stone to the heap under which a criminal lay buried. The Vulgate gives some countenance to this translation: "He who gives honor to a fool is like one who throws a stone to Mercury's heap." Mercury was considered the deity who presided over the highways; and stones were erected in different places to guide the traveler. Hence those lines of Dr. Young: - "Death stands like Mercuries in every way; <div eID="gen24834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24835" type="x-p"/> And kindly points us to our journey's end."
entries.232ff26152f0a7b01068ecdadd97434627b97119: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24836" type="x-p"/> The great God that formed all things - Or, A great man grieveth all, and he hireth the fool, he hireth also transgressors, where this verse is very differently translated. I shall add that of Coverdale: "A man of experience discerneth all thinges well: but whoso hyreth a foole, hyreth soch one as wyl take no hede." The רב rab may mean either the great God, or a great man: hence the two renderings, in the text and in the margin.
entries.3e92855e387acd0c5ef0f66c1efa52a6cd892837: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24837" type="x-p"/> As a dog returneth to his vomit - See note on <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.22">2Pet 2:22</reference>.
entries.552a9d2227fe99f085a7997b8895cc3dc7517dcd: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24838" type="x-p"/> The slothful man saith - See the note on <reference osisRef="Pro.22.13">Pro 22:13</reference> (note).
entries.3c77b7c739b4c2e6c9ba34623bb672ae6933614b: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24839" type="x-p"/> Than seven men that can render a reason - Seven here only means perfection, abundance, or multitude. He is wiser in his own eyes than a multitude of the wisest men. "Than seven men that sytt and teach." - Coverdale; i.e., than seven doctors of the law, or heads of the schools of the prophets, who always sat while they taught.
entries.079065c9074e84235989ae931bcb3cd842350f7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24840" type="x-p"/> He that passeth by - This proverb stands true ninety-nine times out of a hundred, where people meddle with domestic broils, or differences between men and their wives.
entries.e881d0e449a843368262abda4d58144a846eb404: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24841" type="x-p"/> Am not I in sport? - How many hearts have been made sad, and how many reputations have been slain, by this kind of sport! "I designed no harm by what I said;" "It was only in jest," etc. Sportive as such persons may think their conduct to be, it is as ruinous as that of the mad man who shoots arrows, throws firebrands, and projects in all directions instruments of death, so that some are wounded, some burnt, and some slain.
entries.84af0af348cd753db11217877761906fcd6eae22: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen24841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24842" type="x-p"/> Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out - The tale-receiver and the tale-bearer are the agents of discord. If none received the slander in the first instance, it could not be propagated. Hence our proverb, "The receiver is as bad as the thief." And our laws treat them equally; for the receiver of stolen goods, knowing them to be stolen, is hanged, as well as he who stole them.
entries.f223e6df763251cb71b675c18a59291df2dd2cb4: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24843" type="x-p"/> The words of a tale-bearer - The same with <reference osisRef="Pro.18.8">Pro 18:8</reference> (note), where see the note.
entries.7d7c8d86b1d17e2de567f51ab65b255ebbc06114: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24844" type="x-p"/> Burning lips and a wicked heart - Splendid, shining, smooth lips; that is, lips which make great professions of friendship are like a vessel plated over with base metal to make it resemble silver; but it is only a vile pot, and even the outside is not pure.
entries.a932109b6aea974803159fa610512ebc373af12c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24845" type="x-p"/> When he speaketh fair - For there are such hypocrites and false friends in the world. <div eID="gen24845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24846" type="x-p"/> Believe him not - Let all his professions go for nothing. <div eID="gen24846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24847" type="x-p"/> For there are seven abominations in his heart - That is, he is full of abominations.
entries.c325b08be3e050a379a9a30b2842b62cfa0e5e21: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24848" type="x-p"/> Whoso diggeth a pit - See note on <reference osisRef="Psa.7.15">Psa 7:15</reference>. There is a Latin proverb like this: Malum consilium consultori pessimum, "A bad counsel, but worst to the giver." Harm watch; harm catch.
entries.53843044b9e54d9ee7fc2ee48ba9b6ddc73fd807: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24849" type="x-p"/> A lying tongue hateth those that are afflicted by it - He that injures another hates him in proportion to the injury he has done him; and, strange to tell, in proportion to the innocence of the oppressed. The debtor cannot bear the sight of his creditor; nor the knave, of him whom he has injured.  <chapter eID="Prov.26"/> <div eID="gen24849" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b0e6da59719f164b8dfa292415bfd4cfcfe2ab9: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">Pro 26:1</reference> <div eID="gen11685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11686" type="x-p"/> There now follows a group of eleven proverbs of the fool; only the first of the group has after it a proverb of different contents, but of similar form: <div eID="gen11686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11687" type="x-p"/> As snow in summer, and rain in harvest; <div eID="gen11687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11688" type="x-p"/> So honour befitteth not a fool. <div eID="gen11688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11689" type="x-p"/> If there is snow in high summer (קיץ, to be glowing hot), it is contrary to nature; and if there is rain in harvest, it is (according to the alternations of the weather in Palestine) contrary to what is usually the case, and is a hindrance to the ingathering of the fruits of the field. Even so a fool and respect, or a place of honour, are incongruous things; honour will only injure him (as according to <reference osisRef="Prov.19.10">Pro 19:10</reference>, luxury); he will make unjust use of it, and draw false conclusions from it; it will strengthen him in his folly, and only increase it. נאוה (= נאוי) is the adj. to the <hi type="italic">Pil</hi>. נאוה, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.5">Psa 93:5</reference> (plur. נאווּ); נאוה, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.10">Pro 19:10</reference>, and נאוה, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.7">Pro 17:7</reference>, are also masc. and fem. of the adj., according to which, that which is said under <reference osisRef="Prov.19.10">Pro 19:10</reference> is to be corrected. Symmachus and Theodotion have translated οὐκ ἔπρεψεν, and have therefore read נאוה. The root word is נאה (as שׁחה to שׁחוה) = נוה, to aim at something (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Hupfeld under <reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Psa 23:2</reference>).
entries.b0aeb11156eb57e0f35591959e0cbeb135d1e2a3: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.2">Pro 26:2</reference> <div eID="gen11689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11690" type="x-p"/> This verse is formed quite in the same way as the preceding: <div eID="gen11690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11691" type="x-p"/> As the sparrow in its fluttering, as the swallow in its flying, <div eID="gen11691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11692" type="x-p"/> So the curse that is groundless: it cometh not. <div eID="gen11692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11693" type="x-p"/> This passage is one of those fifteen (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>) in which the לא of the text is changed by the Kerı̂ into לו; the Talm., Midrash, and Sohar refer this לּו partly to him who utters the curse himself, against whom also, if he is a judge, such inconsiderate cursing becomes an accusation by God; partly to him who is cursed, for they read from the proverb that the curse of a private person also (הדיוט, ἰδιώτης) is not wont to fall to the ground, and that therefore one ought to be on his guard against giving any occasion for it (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Norzi). But Aben Ezra supposes that לא and לו interchange, as much as to say that the undeserved curse falls on him (לו) who curses, and does not fall (לא) on him who is cursed. The figures in 2a harmonize only with לא, according to which the lxx, the Syr., Targ., <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther (against Jerome) translate, for the principal matter, that the sparrow and the swallow, although flying out (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.8">Pro 27:8</reference>), return home again to their nest (Ralbag), would be left out of view in the comparison by לו. This emphasizes the fluttering and flying, and is intended to affirm that a groundless curse is a פּרח בּאוּיר, aimless, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a thing hovering in the air, that it fails and does not take effect. Most interpreters explain the two <hi type="italic">Lameds</hi> as declaring the destination: <hi type="italic">ut passer</hi> (<hi type="italic">sc. natus est</hi>) <hi type="italic">ad vagandum</hi>, as the sparrow, through necessity of nature, roves about... (Fleischer). But from <reference osisRef="Prov.25.3">Pro 25:3</reference> it is evident that the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in both cases declares the reference or the point of comparison: as the sparrow in respect to its fluttering about, etc. The names of the two birds are, according to Aben Ezra, like dreams without a meaning; but the Romanic exposition explains rightly צפּור by <hi type="italic">passereau</hi>, and דּרור by <hi type="italic">hirondelle</hi>, for צפור (Arab. 'uṣfuwr), twitterer, designates at least preferably the sparrow, and דרור the swallow, from its flight shooting straight out, as it were radiating (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.84.4">Psa 84:4</reference>); the name of the sparrow, dûrı̂ (found in courtyards), which Wetstein, after Saadia, compares to דרור, is etymologically different.<note placement="foot">It is true that the Gemara to <hi type="italic">Negaïm</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.1">Pro 14:1</reference>, explains the Mishnic צפרים דרור, “house-birds,” for it derives דרור from דור, to dwell.</note> <div eID="gen11693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11694" type="x-p"/> Regarding חנּם, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Pro 24:28. Rightly the accentuation separates the words rendered, “so the curse undeserved” (קללת, after Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 79b, קללת), from those which follow; לא תבא is the explication of כן: thus hovering in the air is a groundless curse - it does not come (בוא, like <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Josh.21.43">Jos 21:43</reference>). After this proverb, which is formed like <reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">Pro 26:1</reference>, the series now returns to the “fool.”
entries.877aef1c4f8336132d5edbe8c031dedc1616daf4: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.3">Pro 26:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.3">3</reference> A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass,    And a rod for the back of fools. <div eID="gen11694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11695" type="x-p"/> J. D. Michaelis supposes that the order should be reversed: a bridle for the horse, a whip for the ass; but Arnoldi has here discovered the figure of speech <hi type="italic">merismus</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference>); and Hitzig, in the manner of the division, the rhythmical reason of the combination (cf. שׁם חם ויפת for שׁם יפת וחם): whip and bridle belong to both, for one whips a horse (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.2">Neh 3:2</reference>) and also bridles him; one bridles an ass (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference>) and also whips him (Num 22:28.). As whip and bridle are both serviceable and necessary, so also serviceable and necessary is a rod, לגו כּסילים, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">Pro 10:13</reference>; Pro 19:29.
entries.685e747a43adb46f25a25f830c528d8012a843c8: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.4">Pro 26:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.4">4</reference> Answer not the fool according to his folly,    Lest thou thyself also become like unto him. <div eID="gen11695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11696" type="x-p"/> After, or according to his folly, is here equivalent to recognising the foolish supposition and the foolish object of his question, and thereupon considering it, as if, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, he asked why the ignorant man was happier than the man who had much knowledge, or how one may acquire the art of making gold; for “a fool can ask more than ten wise men can answer.” He who recognises such questions as justifiable, and thus sanctions them, places himself on an equality with the fool, and easily himself becomes one. The proverb that follows affirms apparently the direct contrary:
entries.e5efa6b82be6765c6558abf9ff34541ad6b9e6e8: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.5">Pro 26:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.5">5</reference> Answer the fool according to his folly,    Lest he regard himself as wise. ענה־כסיל (with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Chatef</hi>)<note placement="foot">Thus after Ben Asher; while, on the contrary, Ben Naphtali writes ענה כסיל with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 41.</note> here stands opposed to אל־תען כסיל. The Gospel of John, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Joh 5:31, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">Pro 8:31</reference>,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., my dissertation on three little-observed passages in the Gospel of John, and their practical lessons, in the <hi type="italic">Evang. luth. Kirchenzeitung</hi>, 1869, Nos. 37, 38.</note> is rich in such apparently contradictory sayings. The <hi type="italic">sic et non</hi> here lying before us is easily explained; after, or according to his folly, is this second time equivalent to, as is due to his folly: decidedly and firmly rejecting it, making short work with it (returning a sharp answer), and promptly replying in a way fitted, if possible, to make him ashamed. Thus one helps him, perhaps, to self-knowledge; while, in the contrary case, one gives assistance to his self-importance. The Talmud, <hi type="italic">Schabbath</hi> 30b, solves the contradiction by referring <reference osisRef="Prov.26.4">Pro 26:4</reference> to worldly things, and <reference osisRef="Prov.26.5">Pro 26:5</reference> to religious things; and it is true that, especially in the latter case, the answer is itself a duty toward the fool, and towards the truth. Otherwise the Midrash: one ought not to answer when one knows the fool as such, and to answer when he does not so know him; for in the first instance the wise man would dishonour himself by the answer, in the latter case he would give to him who asks the importance appertaining to a superior.
entries.1866d03e4263f95180f63a95a0dab36aeef7a61b: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.6">Pro 26:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.6">6</reference> He cutteth off the feet, he drinketh injury,    Who transacteth business by a fool. <div eID="gen11696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11697" type="x-p"/> He cutteth off, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, his own feet, as we say: he breaks his neck, <hi type="italic">il se casse le cou</hi>; Lat. <hi type="italic">frangere brachium, crus, coxam; frangere navem</hi> (Fleischer). He thinks to supplement his own two legs by those of the messenger, but in reality he cuts them off; for not only is the commission not carried out, but it is even badly carried out, so that instead of being refreshed (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.17">Pro 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.13">Pro 25:13</reference>) by the quick, faithful execution of it, he has to swallow nothing but damage; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.34.7">Job 34:7</reference>, where, however, drinking scorn is meant of another (lxx), not his own; on the contrary, חמס here refers to injury suffered (as if it were חמדו, for the suff. of חמס is for the most part objective); cf. the similar figures Pro 10:26. So שׁלח בּיד, to accomplish anything by the mediation of another, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.4.13">Exo 4:13</reference>; with דבר (דברים), 2Sa 15:36. The reading מקצּה (Jerome, Luther, <hi type="italic">claudus</hi>) is unnecessary; since, as we saw, מקצּה ,was ew includes it in the <hi type="italic">sibi</hi>. The Syr. reads, after the lxx (the original text of which was ἐκ τῶν ποδῶν ἑαυτοῦ), מקצה, for he errs, as also does the Targumist, in thinking that מקצה can be used for מקצץ; but Hitzig adopts this reading, and renders: “from the end of the legs he swallows injury who sends messages by a fool.” The end of the legs are the feet, and the feet are those of the foolish messenger. The proverb in this form does not want in boldness, but the wisdom which Hitzig finds in its is certainly not mother-wit.<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates שׁתה by ἄνους, so שׁטה (the post-bibl. designation of a fool) - one of the many indications that this translator is a Jew, and as such is not confined in his knowledge of language only to the bibl. Hebrew.</note> <div eID="gen11697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11698" type="x-p"/> Böttcher, on his part, also with מקצה, renders: “from the end of his feet he drinks in that which is bitter...” - that also is too artificial, and is unintelligible without the explanation of its discoverer. But that he who makes a fool his messenger becomes himself like unto one who cuts off his own legs, is a figure altogether excellent.
entries.0f3e3aaaf7f53c1f38abccb891d36a6deea15363: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.7">Pro 26:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.7">7</reference> The hanging down of the legs of a lame man;    And a proverb in a fool’s mouth. <div eID="gen11698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11699" type="x-p"/> With reference to the obscure דּליוּ, the following views have been maintained: - (1) The form as punctuated appears directly as an imperative. Thus the lxx translate, the original text of which is here: ἀφελοῦ πορείαν κυλλῶν (conj. Lagarde’s) καὶ παροιμίαν ἐκ στόματος ἀφρόνων, which the Syr. (with its imitator, the Targ.) has rendered positively: “If thou canst give the power of (sound) going to the lame, then wilt thou also receive (prudent) words from the mouth of a fool.” Since Kimchi, דּליוּ has been regarded by many as the softening of the <hi type="italic">Imp</hi>. <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> דּדּוּ, according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates: ἐπάρατε κνήμας χωλοῦ; and Bertheau and Zöckler explain: always take away his legs from the lame, since they are in reality useless to him, just as a proverb in the mouth of the fool is useless - something that without loss might be never there.” But why did not the poet write הרימוּ, or הסירוּ, or קחוּ, or the like? דּלּי, to carry away, to dispense with, is Syriac (Targ. <hi type="italic">Jer</hi>. I, under <reference osisRef="Deut.32.50">Deu 32:50</reference>), but not Hebrew. And how meaningless is this expression! A lame man would withstand a surgeon (as he would a murderer) who would amputate his legs; for lame legs are certainly better than none, especially since there is a great distinction between a lame man (פּדּח, from פּסח, <hi type="italic">luxare</hi>; cf. (Arab.) fasaḥ, <hi type="italic">laxare</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Schultens) who halts or goes on crutches (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">2Sa 3:29</reference>), and one who is maimed (paralytic), who needs to be carried. It comes to this, that by this rendering of 7a one must, as a consequence, with the lxx, regard וּמשׁל [and a proverb] as object. accus. parallel to שׁקים [legs]; but “to draw a proverb from one’s mouth” is, after <reference osisRef="Prov.20.5">Pro 20:5</reference>, something quite different from to tear a proverb away from him, besides which, one cannot see how it is to be caught. Rather one would prefer: <hi type="italic">attollite crura claudi</hi> (<hi type="italic">ut incedat, et nihil promovebitis</hi>); but the מן of מפּסּח does not accord with this, and 7b does not connect itself with it. But the explanation: “take away the legs from a lame man who has none, at least none to use, and a proverb in the mouth of fools, when there is none,” is shattered against the “leg-taking-away,” which can only be used perhaps of frogs’ legs. (2) Symmachus translates: ἐξέλιπον κνῆμαι ἀπὸ χωλοῦ; and Chajûg explains דּליוּ as 3 pret. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, to which Kimchi adds the remark, that he appears to have found דּליוּ, which indeed is noted by Norzi and J. H. Michaelis as a variant. But the Masoretic reading is דּליוּ, and this, after Gesenius and Böttcher (who in this, without any reason, sees an Ephraimitic form of uttering the word), is a softened variation from דּדּוּ. Only it is a pity that this softening, while it is supported by <hi type="italic">alius</hi> = ἄλλος, <hi type="italic">folium</hi> = φύλλον, faillir = <hi type="italic">fallere</hi>, and the like, has yet not a single Hebrew or Semitic example in its favour. (3) Therefore Ewald finds, “all things considered,” that it is best to read דּליוּ, “the legs are too loose for the lame man to use them.” But, with Dietrich, we cannot concur in this, nor in the more appropriate translation: “the legs of the lame hang down loose,” to say nothing of the clearly impossible: “high are the legs of the lame (one higher than the other),” and that because this form גּליוּ for גּליוּ also occurs without pause, <reference osisRef="Ps.57.2">Psa 57:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Psa 73:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.122.6">Psa 122:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">Isa 21:12</reference>; but although thus, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.32">Psa 68:32</reference>, at the beginning of a clause, yet always only in connection, never at the beginning of an address. (4) It has also been attempted to interpret דּליוּ as abstr., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Euchel: “he learns from a cripple to dance, who seeks to learn proverbs from the mouth of a fool.” דּליוּ שׁקים must mean the lifting up of the legs = springing and dancing. Accordingly Luther translates: “As dancing to a cripple, <div eID="gen11699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11700" type="x-p"/> So does it become a fool to speak of wisdom.” <div eID="gen11700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11701" type="x-p"/> The thought is agreeable, and according to fact; but these words to not mean dancing, but much rather, as the Arabic shows (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Schultens at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.5">Pro 20:5</reference>, and on the passage before us), a limping, waddling walk, like that of ducks, after the manner of a well-bucket dangling to and fro. And דּליוּ, after the form מלכוּ, would be an unheard-of Aramaism. For forms such as שׂחוּ, swimming, and שׁלוּ, security, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">Psa 30:7</reference>, on which C. B. Michaelis and others rest, cannot be compared, since they are modified from sachw, ṣalw, while in דּליוּ the <hi type="italic">û</hi> ending must be, and besides the Aramaic דּליוּ must in <hi type="italic">st. constr</hi>. be דּליוּוּת. Since none of these explanations are grammatically satisfactory, and besides דּליוּ = דּללוּ = דּדּוּ gives a parallel member which is heterogeneous and not conformable to the nature of an emblematical proverb, we read דּלּוּי after the forms צפּוּי, שׁקּוּי (cf. חבּוּק, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.10">Pro 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.33">Pro 24:33</reference>), and this signifies loose, hanging down, from דּלה, to hang at length and loosely down, or transitively: to hang, particularly of the hanging down at length of the bucket-rope, and of the bucket itself, to draw water from the well. The מן is similar to that of <reference osisRef="Job.28.4">Job 28:4</reference>, only that here the connecting of the hanging down, and of that from which it hangs down, is clear. Were we to express the purely nominally expressed emblematical proverb in the form of a comparative one, it would thus stand as Fleischer translates it: <hi type="italic">ut laxa et flaccida dependent</hi> (<hi type="italic">torpent</hi>) <hi type="italic">crura a claudo, sic sententia in ore stultorum</hi> (<hi type="italic">sc. torpet h. e. inutilis est</hi>). The fool can as little make use of an intelligent proverb, or moral maxim (<hi type="italic">dictum sententiosum</hi>), as a lame man can of his feet; the word, which in itself is full of thought, and excellent, becomes halting, lame, and loose in his mouth (Schultens: <hi type="italic">deformiter claudicat</hi>); it has, as spoken and applied by him, neither hand nor foot. Strangely, yet without missing the point, Jerome: <hi type="italic">quomodo pulcras frustra habet claudus tibias, sic indecens est in ore stultorum parabola</hi>. The lame man possibly has limbs that appear sound; but when he seeks to walk, they fail to do him service - so a <hi type="italic">bon-mot</hi> comes forth awkwardly when the fool seeks to make use of it. Hitzig’s conjecture: as leaping of the legs on the part of a lame man..., Böttcher has already shown sufficient reasons for rejecting; leaping on the part of any one, for the leaping of any one, were a court style familiar to no poet.
entries.b10247863baafd8837209aca4757cc311092433a: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.8">Pro 26:8</reference> <div eID="gen11701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11702" type="x-p"/> This proverb presents to us a new difficulty. <div eID="gen11702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11703" type="x-p"/> As one binds a stone in a sling, <div eID="gen11703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11704" type="x-p"/> So is he who giveth honour to a fool. <div eID="gen11704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11705" type="x-p"/> This translation is warranted by tradition, and is in accordance with the actual facts. A sling is elsewhere called קלע; but that מרגּמה also in the passage before us signifies a sling (from רגם, to throw with stones = to stone or to throw stones = to sling, cf. Targ. <reference osisRef="Esth.5.14">Est 5:14</reference> רגּם, of David’s slinging stones against Goliath), is supported by the lxx, Syr., and Targ. on the one side, and the Jewish Glossists on the other (Rashi: <hi type="italic">fronde</hi>, Ital. <hi type="italic">frombola</hi>). Rightly the lxx renders כּצרור as a verb: ὡς ἀποδεσμεύει; on the contrary, the Syr. and Targ. regard it as a substantive: as a piece of stone; but צרור as a substantive does not mean a piece, as one would put into a sling to use as a weapon, but a grain, and thus a little piece, <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.13">2Sa 17:13</reference>; cf. Amo 9:9. Erroneously Ewald: “if one binds to the sling the stone which he yet seeks to throw, then all this throwing and aiming are in vain; so it is in vain to give to a fool honour which does not reach him.” If one seeks to sling a stone, he must lay the <hi type="italic">lapis missilis</hi> so in the sling that it remains firm there, and goes forth only by the strong force of the slinging; this fitting in (of the stone), so that it does not of itself fall out, is expressed by צרר בּ (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Pro 30:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.8">Job 26:8</reference>). The giving is compared to the binding, the stones to the honour, and the sling to the fool: the fool is related to the honour which one confers on him, as the stone to the sling in which one lays it - the giving of honour is a slinging of honour. Otherwise (after Kimchi) the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ὡς συνδεσμὸς λίθου ἐν λιθάδι, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as Fleischer translates: <hi type="italic">ut qui crumenam gemmarum plenam in acervum lapidum conjicit</hi>. Thus also Ralbag, Ahron b. Josef, and others, and lastly Zöckler. The figure is in the form of an address, and מרגּמה (from רגם, <hi type="italic">accumulare, congerere</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Psa 67:1-7 :28) might certainly mean the heaping of stones. But אבן is not used in the sense of אבן יקרה (precious stone); also one does not see why one precious stone is not enough as the figure of honour, and a whole heap is named; but in the third place, כּן נותן requires for כצרור a verbal signification. Therefore Jerome translates: <hi type="italic">sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum Mercurii</hi>; in this the echo of his Jewish teacher, for the Midrash thus explains literally: every one who gives honour to a fool is like one who throws a stone on a heap of stones consecrated to Mercury. Around the Hermes (ἑρμαὶ), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, pillars with the head of Mercury (<hi type="italic">statuae mercuriales</hi> or <hi type="italic">viales</hi>), were heaps of stones (ἕρμακες), to which the passer-by was wont to throw a stone; it was a mark of honour, and served at the same time to improve the way, whose patron was Mercurious (מרקולים). It is self-evident that this Graeco-Roman custom to which the Talm. makes frequent reference, cannot be supposed to have existed in the times of Solomon. Luther translates independently, and apparently rendering into German that in <hi type="italic">acervum Mercurii</hi>: that is as if one threw a precious stone on the “<hi type="italic">Rabenstein</hi>,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the heap of stones raised at the foot of the gallows. This heap of stones is more natural and suitable to the times of Solomon than the heap of stones dedicated to Mercury, if, like Gussetius, one understands מרגמה of a heap of stones, <hi type="italic">supra corpus lapidatum</hi>. But against this and similar interpretations it is enough to remark that כצרור cannot signify <hi type="italic">sicut qui mittit</hi>. Had such a meaning been intended, the word would have been כּהשׁליך or כּמשׁליך. Still different is the rendering of Joseph Kimchi, Aben Ezra, and finally Löwenstein: as when one wraps up a stone in a piece of purple stuff. But ארגּמן, purple, has nothing to do with the verb רגם; it is, as the Aramaic ארגּון shows, a compound word; the supposition of a denom. מרגּמה thus proceeds from a false etymological supposition. And Hitzig’s combination of מרגמה with (Arab.) munjam, handle and beam of a balance (he translates: as a stone on the beam of a balance, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, lies on it), is nothing but refined ingenuity, since we have no need at all of such an Arab. word for a satisfactory clearing up of מרגמה. We abide by the rendering of the sling. Böttcher translates: a sling that scatters; perhaps מרגמה in reality denotes such a sling as throws many stones at once. Let that, however, be as it may: that he who confers a title of honour, a place of honour, and the like, on a fool, is like one who lays a stone in a sling, is a true and intelligibly formed thought: the fool makes the honour no honour; he is not capable of maintaining it; that which is conferred on him is uselessly wasted.
entries.ee5588a6542f1ee40e5eb760a545ae148d780673: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.9">Pro 26:9</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.9">9</reference> A thorn goeth into the hand of a drunkard,    And a proverb in a fool’s mouth;<hi type="italic">i.e</hi>., if a proverb falls into a fool’s mouth, it is as if a thorn entered into the hand of a drunken man; the one is as dangerous as the other, for fools misuse such a proverb, which, rightly used, instructs and improves, only to the wounding and grieving of another, as a drunken man makes use of the pointed instrument which he has possession of for coarse raillery, and as a welcome weapon of his strife. The lxx, Syr. (Targ.?), and Jerome interpret עלה in the sense of shooting up, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of growing; Böttcher also, after <reference osisRef="Prov.24.31">Pro 24:31</reference> and other passages, insists that the thorn which has shot up may be one that has not grown to perfection, and therefore not dangerous. But thorns grow not in the hand of any one; and one also does not perceive why the poet should speak of it as growing in the hand of a drunken man, which the use of the hand with it would only make worse. We have here עלה בידי, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it has come into my hand, commonly used in the Mishna, which is used where anything, according to intention, falls into one’s hands, as well as where it comes accidentally and unsought for, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Nazir </hi> 23a, מי שׁנתכוון לעלות בידו בשׂר חזיר ועלה בידו בשׂר טלה, he who designs to obtain swine’s flesh and (accidentally) obtains lamb’s flesh. Thus rightly Heidenheim, Löwenstein, and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.: ἄκανθα ἀνέβη εἰς χεῖρα μεθύοντος. חוח signifies a thorn bush, 2Ki 14:9,<note placement="foot">The plur. חוחים, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.6">1Sa 13:6</reference>, signifies not thorn bushes, but rock-splitting; in Damascus, chôcha means a little gate in the wing of a large door; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Wetstein’s <hi type="italic">Nordarabien</hi>, p. 23.</note> as well as a thorn, Sol 2:2, but where not the thorns of the rose, and indeed no rose at all, is meant.
