Luther thinks of the rose with the thorn when he explains: “When a drunkard carries and brandishes in his hand a thorn bush, he scratches more with it than allows the roses to be smelled - so a fool with the Scriptures, or a right saying, often does more harm than good.” This paraphrase of Luther’s interprets עלה ביד more correctly than his translation does; on the other hand, the latter more correctly is satisfied with a thorn twig (as a thorn twig which pierces into the hand of a drunken man); the roses are, however, assumed contrary to the text. This holds good also against Wessely’s explanation: “the Mashal is like a rose not without thorns, but in the mouth of a fool is like a thorn without a rose, as when a drunken man seeks to pluck roses and gains by his effort nothing but being pierced by thorns.” The idea of roses is to be rejected, because at the time when this proverb was formed there were no roses in Palestine. The proverb certainly means that a right Mashal, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, an ingenious excellent maxim, is something more and better than a חוח (the prick as of the Jewish thorn, <hi type="italic">Zizyphus vulgaris</hi>, or the <hi type="italic">Christus</hi>-thorn, the <hi type="italic">Ziz spina Christi</hi>); but in the mouth of a fool such a maxim becomes only a useless and a hurtful thing; for the fool so makes use of it, that he only embarrasses others and recklessly does injury to them. The lxx translates משׁל by δουλεία, and the Aram. by שׁטיוּתא; how the latter reached this “folly” is not apparent; but the lxx vocalized משׁל, according to which Hitzig, at the same time changing שׁכּור into שׂכוּר, translates: “thorns shoot up by the hand of the hireling, and tyranny by the mouth of fools.” Although a hired labourer, yet, on this account, he is not devoid of conscience; thus 9a so corrected has something in its favour: one ought, as far as possible, to do all with his own hand; but the thought in 9b is far-fetched, and if Hitzig explains that want of judgment in the state councils creates despotism, so, on the other hand, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.7">Pro 24:7</reference> says that the fool cannot give counsel in the gate, and therefore he holds his mouth.
entries.230a733495ddde1cd80ae1e63978fae9423f98f3: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.10">Pro 26:10</reference> <div eID="gen11705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11706" type="x-p"/> All that we have hitherto read is surpassed in obscurity by this proverb, which is here connected because of the resemblance of ושכר to שכור. We translate it thus, vocalizing differently only one word: <div eID="gen11706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11707" type="x-p"/> Much bringeth forth from itself all; <div eID="gen11707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11708" type="x-p"/> But the reward and the hirer of the fool pass away. <div eID="gen11708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11709" type="x-p"/> The lxx translates πολλὰ χειμάζεται πᾶσα σὰρξ ἀφρόνων (all the flesh of fools suffers much), συντριβήσεται γὰρ ἧ ἔκστασις αὐτῶν, which is in Hebrew: רב מחולל כל בּשׂר כסיל ישּׁבר עברתם <div eID="gen11709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11710" type="x-p"/> An unfortunate attempt so to rectify the words that some meaning might be extracted from them. The first line of this translation has been adopted by the Syr. and Targ., omitting only the כל, in which the self-condemnation of this deciphering lies (for כל בשׂר means elsewhere, humanity, not the whole body of each individual); but they translate the second line as if the words were: ישׁכּר עבר ים<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, and the drunken man sails over the sea (עברים is separated into עבר ים, as בבקרים, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.12">Amo 6:12</reference>, is to be separated into בּבּקר ים); but what does that mean? Does it mean that to a drunkard (but שׁכּור, the drunken man, and not סבא, the drunkard, is used) nothing remains but to wander over the sea? or that the drunken man lets his imagination wander away over the sea, while he neglects the obligation that lies upon him? Symmachus and Theodotion, with the Midrash (Rashi) and Saadia (Kimchi), take שׂכר in 10b = סגר (like <reference osisRef="Isa.19.10">Isa 19:10</reference>, שׂכר = embankment, cf. סכּרין, <hi type="italic">Kelim</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Pro 23:5</reference>); the former translates by καὶ ὁ φράσσων ἄφρονα ἐμφράσσει τὰς ὀργὰς αὐτοῦ, the latter by καὶ φιμῶν ἄφρονα φιμοῖ χόλους, yielding to the imagination that עברים, like עברות, may be the plur. of עברה, anger. Jerome punctuates רב as, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.8">Pro 25:8</reference>, רב, and interprets, as Symmachus and Theodotion, שׂכר both times = סגר, translating: <hi type="italic">Judicium determinat causas, et qui imponit stulto silentium iras mitigat</hi>; but רב does not mean <hi type="italic">judicium</hi>, nor מחולל <hi type="italic">determinat</hi>, nor כל <hi type="italic">causas</hi>. As Gussetius, so also Ralbag (in the first of his three explanations), Meîri, Elia Wilna interpret the proverb as a declaration regarding quarrelsome persons: he causeth woe to all, and hireth fools, hireth transgressors, for his companions; but in that case we must read רב for רב; מחולל, bringing woe, would be either the <hi type="italic">Po</hi>. of חלל, to bore through, or <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> of חיל (חוּל), to put into distress (as with pangs); but עברים, transgressors = sinners, is contrary to the O.T. <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">Pro 22:3</reference> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.12">Pro 27:12</reference>) is falsely cited in its favour; besides, for רב there should have been at least אישׁ רב and why שׂכרו is repeated remains inexplicable. Others take מחולל־כל as the name of God, the creator of all men and things; and truly this is the nearest impression of these two words, for חולל is the usual designation for divine production, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Psa 90:2. Accordingly Kimchi explains: The Lord is the creator of all, and He gives to fools and to transgressors their maintenance; but עברים, transgressors, is Mishnic, not bibl.; and שׂכר means to hire, but not to supply with food. The proverb is thus incapable of presenting a thought like <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mat 5:45</reference> (He maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good). Others translate: “The Lord is creator of all, and takes fools, takes idlers, into His service.” Thus rendered, the proverb is offensive; wherefore Rashi, Moses Kimchi, Arama, and others regard the Mashal as in the mouth of fools, and thus they take <reference osisRef="Prov.26.9">Pro 26:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.26.10">Pro 26:10</reference> together as a tetrastich. Certainly this second collection of proverbs contains also tetrastiches; but <reference osisRef="Prov.26.9">Pro 26:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.26.10">Pro 26:10</reference> cannot be regarded as together forming a tetrastich, because רב (which is valid against Kimchi also) cannot mean God the Lord: רב, Lord, is unheard of in bibl. Heb., and at least the word הרב must be used for God. The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. on this account does not follow Kimchi, but translates, Ἄρχων πλάττει πάντα, καὶ μισθοῦται μωρὸν καὶ μισθοῦται ὡς παραβάτης (ought to have been παραβάτας); but who could this cunning man be? Perhaps the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. is to be understood, after Gecatilia (in Rashi): a great (rich) man performs all manner of things; but if he hires a fool, it is as if he hired the first best who pass along the way. But that חולל is used in the general sense of to execute, to perform, is without example, and improbable. Also the explanation: a ruler brings grief, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, severe oppression, upon all (Abulwalîd, Immanuel, Aben Ezra, who, in his smaller grammar, explains רב = רב after <reference osisRef="Isa.49.9">Isa 49:9</reference>; C. B. Michaelis: <hi type="italic">dolore afficit omnes</hi>), does not recommend itself; for חולל, whether it be from חלל, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference> (to bore through), or from חיל, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.9">Psa 29:9</reference> (to bring on the pangs of birth), is too strong a word for hurting; also the clause, thus generally understood, is fortunately untrue. Translated as by Euchel: “the prominent persons destroy all; they keep fools in pay, and favour vagabonds,” - it sounds as if it had been picked up in an assembly of democrats. On the other hand, the proverb, as translated by Luther: <div eID="gen11710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11711" type="x-p"/> A good master maketh a thing right; <div eID="gen11711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11712" type="x-p"/> But he who hireth a bungler, by him it is spoiled, is worthy of the Book of Proverbs. The second line is here freely rendered, but it is also appropriate, if we abide closer by the words of the text, in this connection. Fleischer: <hi type="italic">Magister</hi> (<hi type="italic">artifex peritus</hi>) <hi type="italic">effingit omnia</hi> (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">bene perficit quaecunque ei committuntur</hi>); <hi type="italic">qui autem stultum conducit, conducit transeuntes</hi> (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">idem facit ac si homines ignotos et forte transeuntes ad opus gravius et difficilius conduceret</hi>). Thus also Gesenius, Böttcher, and others, who all, as Gecatilia above, explain עברים, τοὺς τυχόντας, the first best. But we are reluctantly constrained to object to this thought, because רב nowhere in bibl. Hebrew signifies a master; and the ו of the second ושׂכר dno cannot bear that rendering, <hi type="italic">ac si</hi>. And if we leave it out, we nevertheless encounter a difficulty in חולל, which cannot be used of human production. Many Christian interpreters (Cocceius, Schultens, Schelling, Ewald, Bertheau, Stier, Zöckler) give to רב a meaning which is found in no Jewish interpreter, viz., <hi type="italic">sagittarius</hi>, from רבב (רבב), <reference osisRef="Gen.49.23">Gen 49:23</reference> (and perhaps <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">Psa 18:15</reference>), after the forms צר, שׂר, the plur. of which, רבּים, is found at <reference osisRef="Job.16.13">Job 16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jer 50:29</reference>, but in a connection which removes all doubt from the meaning of the word. Here also רב may be more closely defined by מחולל; but how then does the proverb stand? “an archer who wounds everything, and he who hires a fool, and hires passers-by” (Ewald: street-runners), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, they are alike. But if the archer piercing everything is a comic <hi type="italic">Hercules furens</hi>, then, in order to discover the resemblance between the three, there is need of a portion of ingenuity, such as is only particularly assigned to the favoured. But it is also against the form and the usage of the word to interpret עברים simply of rogues and vagabonds. Several interpreters have supposed that רב and כל must stand in a certain interchangeable relation to each other. Thus, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ahron b. Josef: “Much makes amazement to all, but especially one who hires a fool....” But this “especially” (Before all) is an expression smuggled in. Agreeing with Umbreit and Hitzig, we translate line first; but in translating line second, we follow our own method: <div eID="gen11712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11713" type="x-p"/> Much bringeth all out of it;<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, where there is much, then one has it in his power, if he begins right, to undertake everything. רב has by כּל the definition of a neuter, so as to designate not only many men, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.21">Exo 19:21</reference>, but also much ability in a pecuniary and facultative sense (cf. the subst. רב, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Isa 63:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.7">Psa 145:7</reference>); and of the much which bringeth forth all out of itself, effects all by itself, חולל with equal right might be used, as <reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pro 25:23</reference>, of the north wind. The antithesis 10b takes this form: <div eID="gen11713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11714" type="x-p"/> But the reward (read וּשׂכר) and the master (who hires him for wages) of the fool pass away,<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, perish; עברים, as if עבר, is used of chaff, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5">Isa 29:5</reference>; of stubble, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.24">Jer 13:24</reference>; of shadow, Psa 144:4. That which the fool gains passes away, for he squanders it; and he who took him into his service for wages is ruined along with him, for his work is only pernicious, not useful. Although he who possesses much, and has great ability, may be able to effect everything of himself, yet that is not the case when he makes use of the assistance therein of foolish men, who not only do not accomplish anything, but, on the contrary, destroy everything, and are only ruinous to him who, with good intention, associates them with himself in his work. That the word must be more accurately ושׂכר, instead of ושׂכרוו, one may not object, since ושׂכר is perfectly unambiguous, and is manifestly the object.
entries.9f39c1389d278e3ed1695c4aa18d3da25f7c3a8d: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pro 26:11</reference> <div eID="gen11714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11715" type="x-p"/> The series of proverbs regarding fools is continued: <div eID="gen11715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11716" type="x-p"/> Like a dog which returneth to his vomit, <div eID="gen11716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11717" type="x-p"/> Is a fool who cometh again with his folly. שׁב is like שׁונה, particip.; only if the punctuation were כּכּלב, ought “which returneth to his vomit” to be taken as a relative clause (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.38.14">Psa 38:14</reference>). Regarding על as designating the <hi type="italic">terminus quo</hi> with verbs of motions, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Köhler under Mal. 3:24. On קא = קיא, cf. Pro 23:8. Luther rightly; as a dog devours again his vomit. The lxx translate: ὥσπερ κύων ὅταν ἐπέλθῃ ἐπὶ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἔμετον; the reference in 2Pe 2:22 : κύων ἐπιστρέψας ἐπὶ τὸ ἴδιον ἐξέραμα, is thus not from the lxx; the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. is not connected with this N.T. citation, but with the lxx, if its accordance with it is not merely accidental. To devour again its vomit is common with the dog.<note placement="foot">Vid., Schulze’s <hi type="italic">Die bibl. Sprichwörter der deutschen Sprache</hi>, p. 71f.</note> <div eID="gen11717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11718" type="x-p"/> Even so, it is the manner of fools to return again in word and in deed to their past folly (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding שׁנה with ב of the object. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.9">Pro 17:9</reference>); as an Aram. popular saying has it: the fool always falls back upon his foolish conduct.<note placement="foot">Vid., Wahl’s <hi type="italic">Das Sprichwort der heb.-aram. Literatur</hi>, p. 147; Duke’s <hi type="italic">Rabbin. Blumenlese</hi>, p. 9.</note> <div eID="gen11718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11719" type="x-p"/> He must needs do so, for folly has become to him a second nature; but this “must” ceases when once a divine light shines forth upon him. The lxx has after <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pro 26:11</reference> a distich which is literally the same as Sir. 4:21.
entries.7787ae074f78ce972de296993e0978ba16019e6b: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">Pro 26:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">12</reference> Seest thou a man who is wise in his own eyes?      The fool hath more hope than he. <div eID="gen11719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11720" type="x-p"/> Regarding the <hi type="italic">perf. hypotheticum</hi> ראית, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 22:29. Line second is repeated, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.20">Pro 29:20</reference>, unchanged. ממּנּוּ, <hi type="italic">prae eo</hi>, is equivalent to the Mishnic יותר ממּנּוּ, <hi type="italic">plus quam ei</hi>. As the conversion of a sinner, who does not regard himself as righteous, is more to be expected than that of a self-righteous man (Mat 9:12.), so the putting right of a fool, who is conscious that he is not wise (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.7">Pro 24:7</reference>), is more likely to be effected than that of one deeming himself wise; for the greatest hindrance to any turning toward that which is better lies in the delusion that he does not need it.<note placement="foot">The Targum has 12b after Codd. פּקח סכלא טב מגּיהּ (= Syr. pekach, <hi type="italic">expedit, convenit, melius est</hi>), it is far better circumstanced regarding the fool than regarding him. <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Geiger’s <hi type="italic">Zeitschr</hi>. vi. (1868), p. 154.</note> <div eID="gen11720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11721" type="x-p"/> Thus far the group of proverbs regarding fools.
entries.0ec1b6f76ad6fb4b4fd949f8904db0772b8e7d53: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.13">Pro 26:13</reference> <div eID="gen11721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11722" type="x-p"/> There follows now a group of proverbs regarding the slothful: 13 The slothful saith there is a lion without,      A lion in the midst of the streets; cf. the original of this proverb, Pro 22:13. שׁוּעל, to say nothing of שׁחל, is not the jackal; שׁחל is the bibl. name for the lion. בּין is the more general expression for בּקרב, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference>; by the streets he thinks of the rows of houses that form them.
entries.3ecd0c21614d0ae7f456ac04ee08ca57e8377df4: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.14">Pro 26:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.14">14</reference> The door turneth on its hinges,      And the sluggard on his bed. <div eID="gen11722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11723" type="x-p"/> The comparison is clear. The door turns itself on its hinges, on which it hangs, in and out, without passing beyond the narrow space of its motion; so is the fool on his bed, where he turns himself from the one side to the other. He is called עצל, because he is fast glued to the place where he is (Arab. 'azila), and cannot be free (contrast of the active, cf. Arab. ḥafyf, moving nimbly, <hi type="italic">agilis</hi>). But the door offers itself as a comparison, because the diligent goes out by it to begin his work without (<reference osisRef="Prov.24.27">Pro 24:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.23">Psa 104:23</reference>), while the sluggard rolls himself about on his bed. The hook, the hinge, on which the door is moved, called ציר, from צוּר, to turn,<note placement="foot">The Arab. verb signifies radically: to turn, like the Persian verbs kashatn and kardydan, and like our “<hi type="italic">werden</hi>” to grow, turn, accords with <hi type="italic">vertere</hi> (Fleischer).</note> has thus the name of הסּוב.
entries.3156002e8b8400351e27a804401233b696abfff6: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.15">Pro 26:15</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.15">15</reference> The slothful has thrust his hand into the dish,      It is hard for him to bring it back to his mouth again. <div eID="gen11723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11724" type="x-p"/> A variation of <reference osisRef="Prov.19.24">Pro 19:24</reference>; the fut. ישׁיבנּה there, is here explained by נלאה להשׁיבהּ.
entries.6673b0f4dbecd4eef67cf00951864923f0957ac4: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.16">Pro 26:16</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.16">16</reference> The sluggard is wise in his own eyes,      More than seven men who give an excellent answer. <div eID="gen11724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11725" type="x-p"/> Between slothfulness and conceit there exists no inward necessary mutual relation. The proverb means that the sluggard as such regards himself as wiser than seven, who all together answer well at any examination: much labour - he thinks with himself - only injures the health, blunts men for life and its joys, leads only to over-exertion; for the most prudent is, as a general rule, crack-brained. Böttcher’s “<hi type="italic">maulfaule</hi>” [slow to speak] belongs to the German style of thinking; עטל לשׁנא in Syr. is not he who is slow to speak, but he who has a faltering tongue.<note placement="foot">The Aram. עטל is the Hebr. עצל, as עטא = עצה; but in Arab. corresponds not to 'atal, but to 'azal.</note> <div eID="gen11725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11726" type="x-p"/> Seven is the number of manifoldness in completed unfolding (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Pro 9:1</reference>). Meîri thinks, after Ezr 7:14, on the council of seven of the Asiatic ruler. But seven is a round number of plurality, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.25">Pro 26:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.16">Pro 24:16</reference>; Pro 6:31. Regarding טעם, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 11:22.
entries.16df0c10d78b63d8e5dfb5acc18863bfb4da618c: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.17">Pro 26:17</reference> <div eID="gen11726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11727" type="x-p"/> A series of proverbs which recommend the love of peace, for they present caricatures of the opposite: 17 He seizeth by the ears of a dog passing by,      Who is excited by a strife which concerns him not. <div eID="gen11727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11728" type="x-p"/> According to the accentuation in the text, the proverb is to be translated with Fleischer: <hi type="italic">Qualis est qui prehendit aures canis, talis est qui forte transiens ira abripitur propter rixam alienam</hi> (<hi type="italic">eique temere se immiscent</hi>). Since he is cautioned against unwarranted interference, the expression מתערב בּדין might have been used (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.10">Pro 14:10</reference>), according to which the Syr. translates; but על־ריב substantiates the originality of מתעבּר (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.14.16">Pro 14:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.2">Pro 20:2</reference>). On the other hand, the placing together, without any connection of the two participles, is perplexing; why not עבר וּמתעבּר? For it is certainly not meant, that falling into a passion he passes by; but that passing by, he falls into a passion; for he stands to this object. The Targumist, feeling this also, renders עבר in the sense of being angry, but contrary to the <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>. Wherefore the conjecture of Euchel and Abramsohn commends itself, that עבר belongs to כלב - the figure thereby becomes more distinct. To seize one’s own dog by the ear is not dangerous, but it is not advisable to do this with a strange dog. Therefore עבר belongs as a necessary attribute to the dog. The dog accidentally passing by corresponds to the strife to which one stands in no relation (ריב לא־ול, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, Baer’s <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 85, not. 9). Whoever is excited to passion about a strife that does not belong to him, is like one who lays hold by the ears (the lxx arbitrarily: by the tail) of a dog that is passing by - to the one or to the other it happens right when he brings evil upon himself thereby.
entries.d96095b0b9c7cffa9ad04b8a5679ba7607e7f12b: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.18-Prov.26.19">Pro 26:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen11728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11729" type="x-p"/> These verses form a tetrastich: 18 As a man who casteth brands,      And arrows, and death; 19 So is the man who deceiveth his neighbour,      And saith: I only make sport. <div eID="gen11729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11730" type="x-p"/> The old translations of מתלהלה are very diverse. Aquila has rendered it by κακοηθιζόμενος; Symmachus: πειρώμενοι; the Syr.: the vainglorious; the Targ.: מתּחת (from נחת), a successor (spiritually); Jerome: <hi type="italic">noxius</hi> (injurious; for which Luther: secret). There is thus no traditional translation. Kimchi explains the word by השׁתגע (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἐξεστώς); Aben Ezra by השׁתטה (from שׂטה), to behave thoughtlessly, foolishly; but both erroneously, confounding with it ותּלהּ, <reference osisRef="Gen.47.13">Gen 47:13</reference>, which is formed from להה and not from לההּ, and is related to לאה, according to which מתלהלה would designate him who exerts himself (Rashi, המתיגע), or who is worn out (Saadia: who does not know what to do, and in weariness passes his time). The root לההּ (להּ), whence the reflex form התלהלהּ, like התמהמהּ, from מההּ, מהּ) leads to another primary idea. The root להּ presents in (Arab.) âliha (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer in the <hi type="italic">Comm. zur Genesis</hi>, p. 57), waliha, and taliha, formed from the 8th form of this verb (aittalah), the fundamental meaning of internal and external unrest; these verbs are used of the effect of fear (shrinking back from fear), and, generally, the want of self-command; the Syr. otlahlah, to be terrified, <hi type="italic">obstupescere</hi>, confirms this primary conception, connecting itself with the R. להּ. Accordingly, he who shoots every possible death-bringing arrow, is thought of as one who is beside himself, one who is of confused mind, in which sense the passive forms of (Arab.) âlah and talah are actually used. Schultens’ reference to (Arab.) lâh <hi type="italic">micare</hi>, according to which כמתלהלה must mean <hi type="italic">sicut ludicram micationem exercens</hi> (Böttcher: one who exerts himself; Malbim: one who scoffs, from התל), is to be rejected, because מתלהלה must be the direct opposite of משׂחק; and Ewald’s comparison of (Arab.) wâh and akhkh, to be entangled, distorted, lâh, to be veiled, confounds together heterogeneous words. Regarding זקּים (from זנק), burning arrows, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Isa 50:11. Death stands third, not as comprehensive (that which is deadly of every kind), but as a climax (yea, even death itself). The כּן of the principal sentence, correlate to כּ of the contiguous clause, has the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> in our editions; but the laws of the metrical <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> require כּן אישׁ (with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>), as it occurs <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in Cod. 1294. A man who gives vent to his malice against his neighbour, and then says: seest thou not that... (הלא, like Arab. âlâ), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, I am only jesting, I have only a joke with thee: he exhibits himself as being mad, who in blind rage scatters about him deadly arrows.
entries.91f9576de10063d4c98e66a4459897f0443ef541: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.20">Pro 26:20</reference> <div eID="gen11730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11731" type="x-p"/> There now follow proverbs regarding the nirgân, the slanderer (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding the formation and import of this word at <reference osisRef="Prov.26.28">Pro 26:28</reference>): <reference osisRef="Prov.26.20">20</reference> Where the wood faileth, the fire goeth out;      And where no tale-bearer, discord cometh to silence. <div eID="gen11731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11732" type="x-p"/> Wood, as material for building or for burning, is called, with the plur. of its product, עצים. Since אפס is the absolute end of a thing, and thus expresses its no longer existing, so it was more appropriate to wood (Fleischer: <hi type="italic">consumtis lignis</hi>) than to the tale-bearer, of whom the proverb says the same thing as <reference osisRef="Prov.22.10">Pro 22:10</reference> says of the mocker.
entries.f394541e8bfcc681b2cb7cef419531a420a23b9a: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.21">Pro 26:21</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.21">21</reference> Black coal to burning coal, and wood to fire;      And a contentious man to stir up strife. <div eID="gen11732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11733" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates פּחם by καρβών, and גּחלת by ἄνθραξ; the former (from פּחם, Arab. faḥuma, to be deep black) is coal in itself; the latter (from גּחל, jaham, to set on fire, and intrans. to burn), coal in a glowing state (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.22">Pro 25:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.13">Eze 1:13</reference>). Black coal is suited to glowing coal, to nourish it; and wood to the fire, to sustain it; and a contentious man is suited for and serves this purpose, to kindle up strife. חרר signifies to be hot, and the <hi type="italic">Pilpel</hi> חרחר, to heat, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to make hot or hotter. The three - coal, wood, and the contentious man - are alike, in that they are a means to an end.
entries.465ccfaace509b405c8dbf7029bc3142b9e7b36b: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.22">Pro 26:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.22">22</reference> The words of the tale-bearer are like dainty morsels;      And they glide down into the innermost parts. <div eID="gen11733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11734" type="x-p"/> A repetition of Pro 18:8.
entries.084312ec2f8e0fc4dc8fcbf96da7118b905dd781: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.23">Pro 26:23</reference> <div eID="gen11734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11735" type="x-p"/> The proverbs next following treat of a cognate theme, hypocrisy (the art of dissembling), which, under a shining [<hi type="italic">gleissen</hi>] exterior,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., regarding <hi type="italic">gleisen</hi> (to give a deceitful appearance) and <hi type="italic">gleissen</hi> (to throw a dazzling appearance), Schmitthenner-Weigand’s <hi type="italic">Deutsches Wörterbuch</hi>.</note> conceals hatred and destruction: 23 Dross of silver spread over an earthen vessel -      Lips glowing with love and a base heart. <div eID="gen11735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11736" type="x-p"/> Dross of silver is the so-called <hi type="italic">glätte</hi> (French, <hi type="italic">litharge</hi>), a combination of lead and oxygen, which, in the old process of producing silver, was separated (Luther: <hi type="italic">silberschaum</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the silver <hi type="italic">litharge</hi>; Lat. <hi type="italic">spuma argenti</hi>, having the appearance of foam). It is still used to glaze over potter’s ware, which here (Greek, κέραμος) is briefly called חרשׂ for כּלי חרשׂ; for the vessel is better in appearance than the mere potsherd. The glossing of the earthenware is called צפּה על־חרשׂ, which is applicable to any kind of covering (צפּה, R. צף, to spread or lay out broad) of a less costly material with that which is more precious. 23a contains the figure, and 23b its subscription: שׂפתים דּלקים ולב רע. Thus, with the taking away of the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> after Codd., to be punctuated: burning lips, and therewith a base heart; burning, that is, with the fire of love (Meîri, אשׁ החשׁק), while yet the assurances of friendship, sealed by ardent kisses, serve only to mask a far different heart. The lxx translate דלקים [burning] by λεῖα, and thus have read חלקים [smooth], which Hitzig without reason prefers; burning lips (Jerome, incorrectly: <hi type="italic">tumentia</hi>; Luther, after <reference osisRef="Deut.32.33">Deu 32:33</reference>, חמת: <hi type="italic">Gifftiger mund</hi> = a poisonous mouth) are just flattering, and at the same time hypocritical<note placement="foot">Schultens explains the <hi type="italic">labia flagrantia</hi> by <hi type="italic">volubiliter prompta et diserta</hi>. But one sees from the Arab. dhaluḳa, to be loose, lightly and easily moved (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., in Fleischer’s <hi type="italic">Beiträgen zur arab. Sprachkunde</hi> the explanation of the designation of the liquid expressed with the point of the tongue by dhalḳiytt, at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.26-Prov.1.27">Pro 1:26-27</reference>; cf. de Sacy’s <hi type="italic">Grammar</hi>), and dalḳ, to draw out (of the sword from its scabbard), to rinse (of water), that the meaning of the Heb. דלק, to burn, from R. דל, refers to the idea of the flickering, tongue-like movement of the flame.</note> lips. Regarding שׂפתים as masc., <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 85; לב רע means, at <reference osisRef="Prov.25.20">Pro 25:20</reference>, <hi type="italic">animus maestus</hi>; here, <hi type="italic">inimicus</hi>. The figure is excellent: one may regard a vessel with the silver gloss as silver, and it is still earthen; and that also which gives forth the silver glance is not silver, but only the refuse of silver. Both are suitable to the comparison: the lips only glitter, the heart is false (Heidenheim).
entries.56df5c18fa17b2cbaa353f6b4c027b37ebd39e46: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.24-Prov.26.25">Pro 26:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen11736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11737" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.24">Pro 26:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.26.25">Pro 26:25</reference> form a tetrastich. 24 With his lips the hater dissembleth,      And in his heart he museth deceit. 25 If he maketh his voice agreeable, believe him not,      For seven abominations are in his heart. <div eID="gen11737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11738" type="x-p"/> All the old translators (also the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. and Luther) give to יגּכר the meaning, to become known; but the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. as well as the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.11">Pro 20:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.47.17">Gen 47:17</reference>) unites with this meaning also the meaning to make oneself known: to make oneself unknown, unrecognisable = (Arab.) tanakkr, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, by means of clothing, or by a changed expression of countenance.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., de Goeje’s <hi type="italic">Fragmenta Hist. Arab</hi>. ii. (1871), p. 94. The verb נכר, primarily to fix one’s attention, sharply to contemplate anything, whence is derived the meanings of knowing and of not knowing, disowning. The account of the origin of these contrasted meanings, in Gesenius-Dietrich’s <hi type="italic">Lexicon</hi>, is essentially correct; but the Arab. nakar there referred to means, not sharpness of mind, from nakar = הכּיר, but from the negative signification prevailing in the Arab. alone, a property by which one makes himself worthy of being disowned: craftiness, cunning, and then also <hi type="italic">in bonam partem</hi>: sagacity.</note> <div eID="gen11738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11739" type="x-p"/> The contrast demands here this latter signification: <hi type="italic">labiis suis alium se simulat osor, intus in pectore autem reconditum habet dolum</hi> (Fleischer). This rendering of ישׁית מרמה is more correct than Hitzig’s (“in his breast) he prepares treachery;” for שׁית מרמה is to be rendered after שׁית עצות, <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">Psa 13:3</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Hupfeld’s and also our comm. on this passage), not after <reference osisRef="Jer.9.7">Jer 9:7</reference>; for one says שׁית מוקשׁים, to place snares, שׁית ארב, to lay an ambush, and the like, but not to place or to lay deceit. If such a dissembler makes his voice agreeable (<hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of חנן only here, for the form <reference osisRef="Ps.9.14">Psa 9:14</reference> is, as it is punctuated, <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>), trust not thyself to him (האמין, with ב: to put firm trust in anything, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 312)<note placement="foot">The fundamental idea of firmness in האמין is always in the subject, not the object. The Arabic interpreters remark that âman with ב expresses recognition, and with ל submission (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lane’s <hi type="italic">Lexicon</hi> under âman); but in Hebr. האמין with ב <hi type="italic">fiducia fidei</hi>, with ל <hi type="italic">assensus fidei</hi>; the relation is thus not altogether the same.</note> for seven abominations, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a whole host of abominable thoughts and designs, are in his heart; he is, if one may express it, after <reference osisRef="Matt.12.45">Mat 12:45</reference>, possessed inwardly of seven devils. The lxx makes a history of 24a: an enemy who, under complaints, makes all possible allowances, but in his heart τεκταίνεται δόλους. The history is only too true, but it has no place in the text.
entries.61624d9ac89ca8d49649184b88a1d94c2cb29991: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.26">Pro 26:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.26">26</reference> Hatred may conceal itself behind deceit:      Its wickedness shall be exposed in the assembly. <div eID="gen11739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11740" type="x-p"/> Proverbs which begin with the fut. are rarely to be found, it is true; yet, as we have seen, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.26">Pro 12:26</reference>, they are sometimes to be met with in the collection. This is one of the few that are of such a character; for that the lxx and others translate ὁ κρύπτων, which gives for רעתו a more appropriate reference, does not require us to agree with Hitzig in reading הכּסה (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.16">Pro 12:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.23">Pro 12:23</reference>) - the two clauses rendered fut. stand in the same syntactical relation, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Job 20:24. Still less can the rendering of במשׁאון by συνίστησι δόλον, by the lxx, induce us to read with Hitzig חרשׁ און, especially since it is doubtful whether the Heb. words which floated before those translators (the lxx) have been fallen upon. משּׁאון (beginning and ending with a formative syllable) is certainly a word of rare formation, to be compared only to מסדּרון, Jdg 3:23; but since the nearest-lying formation משּׁא signifies usury (from נשׁא, to credit) (according to which Symmachus, διὰ λήμματα, to desire gain), it is obvious that the language preferred this double formation for the meaning deceiving, illusion, or, exactly: fraud. It may also be possible to refer it, like משּׁוּאות (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Psa 23:1-6 :18), to שׁוא = שׁאה, to be confused, waste, as this is done by Parchon, Kimchi (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἐν ἐρημίᾳ), Ralbag, and others; משׁאון, in this sense of deepest concealment, certainly says not a little as the contrast of קהל [an assembly], but ישׁימום [a desert] stood ready for the poet to be used in this sense; he might also have expressed himself as <reference osisRef="Job.30.3">Job 30:3</reference>; Job 38:27. The selection of this rare word is better explained if it denotes the superlative of deceit - a course of conduct maliciously directed toward the deception of a neighbour. That is also the impression which the word has made on Jerome (<hi type="italic">fraudulenter</hi>), the Targ. (בּמוּרסתא, in grinding), Luther (to do injury), and according to which it has already been explained, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, by C. B. Michaelis and Oetinger (“with dissembled, deceitful nature”). The punctuation of תכסה, Codd. and editions present in three different forms. Buxtorf in his <hi type="italic">Concordance</hi> (also Fürst), and the Basel <hi type="italic">Biblia Rabbinica</hi>, have the form תּכסּה; but this is a mistake. Either תּכּסה (<hi type="italic">Niph</hi>.) תּכּסּה (<hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>., with the same assimilation of the preformative ת as in הכּבּס, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.55">Lev 13:55</reference>; נכּפּר, <reference osisRef="Deut.21.8">Deu 21:8</reference>) is to be read; Kimchi, in his <hi type="italic">Wörterbuch</hi>, gives תּכּסּה, which is certainly better supported. A surer contrast of במשׁאון and בקהל remains in our interpretation; only we translate not as Ewald: “hatred seeks to conceal itself by hypocrisy,” but: in deceitful work. Also we refer רעתו, not to במשׁאון, but to שׂנאה, for hatred is thought of in connection with its personal representative. We see from 26b that hatred is meant which not only broods over evil, but also carries it into execution. Such hatred may conceal itself in cunningly-contrived deception, yet the wickedness of the hater in the end comes out from behind the mask with the light of publicity.
entries.5e7858d3c67634c8186c0408ba71fbffd7790704: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.27">Pro 26:27</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.27">27</reference> He who diggeth a pit falleth therein;      And he that rolleth up a stone, upon himself it rolleth back. <div eID="gen11740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11741" type="x-p"/> The thought that destruction prepared for others recoils upon its contriver, has found its expression everywhere among men in divers forms of proverbial sayings; in the form which it here receives, 27a has its oldest original in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>, whence it is repeated here and in <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.8">Ecc 10:8</reference>, and Sir. 27:26. Regarding כּרה, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 16:27. בּהּ here has the sense of <hi type="italic">in eam ipsam</hi>; expressed in French, the proverb is: <hi type="italic">celui qui creuse la fosse, y tombera</hi>; in Italian: <hi type="italic">chi cava la fossa, caderà in essa</hi>. The second line of this proverb accords with <reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Hupfeld and Riehm on this passage). It is natural to think of the rolling as a rolling upwards; cf. Sir. 27:25, ὁ βάλλων λίθον εἰς ὕψος ἐπὶ κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ βάλλει, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, throws it on his own head. וגלל אבן is to be syntactically judged of like Pro 18:13.
entries.8d65ac8ddb5f46ab204b33139320fa35249cfea5: <reference osisRef="Prov.26.28">Pro 26:28</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.28">28</reference> The lying tongue hateth those whom it bruiseth;      And a flattering mouth causeth ruin. <div eID="gen11741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11742" type="x-p"/> The lxx, Jerome, the Targ., and Syr. render ישׂנא דכיו in the sense of <hi type="italic">non amat veritatem</hi>; they appear by דכיו to have thought of the Aram. דכיא, that which is pure; and thus they gain nothing else but an undeniable plain thought. Many Jewish interpreters gloss: מוכיחיו, also after the Aram.: דּכּיו = מדכּיו; but the Aram. דּכּי does not mean pure in the sense of being right, therefore Elia Wilna understands him who desires to justify himself, and this violent derivation from the Aram. thus does not lead to the end. Luther, translating: “a false tongue hates those who punish it,” explains, as also Gesenius, <hi type="italic">conterentes</hi> = <hi type="italic">castigantes ipsam</hi>; but דּך signifies, according to the usage of the language before us, “bruised” (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>), not: bruising; and the thought that the liar hates him who listens to him, leads <hi type="italic">ad absurdum</hi>; but that he does not love him who bruises (punishes) him, is self-evident. Kimchi sees in דּכּיו another form of דּכּא; and Meîri, Jona Gerundi in his ethical work (שׁערי תשׁובה = The gates of Repentance), and others, accordingly render דכיו in the sense of ענו (עניו): the lying tongue hates - as Löwenstein translates - the humble [pious]; also that for דכּיו, by the omission of ו, דכּי = זכּי may be read, is supposable; but this does not harmonize with the second half of the proverb, according to which לשׁון שׁקר must be the subject, and ישׂנא דכיו must express some kind of evil which proceeds from such a tongue. Ewald: “the lying tongue hates its master (אדניו),” but that is not in accordance with the Heb. style; the word in that case should have been בּעליו. Hitzig countenances this אדניו, with the remark that the tongue is here personified; but personified, the tongue certainly means him who has it (<reference osisRef="Ps.120.3">Psa 120:3</reference>). Böttcher’s conjecture ישׁנּא דכיו, “confounds their talk,” is certainly a curiosity. Spoken of the sea, those words would mean, “it changes its surge.” But is it then at all necessary to uncover first the meaning of 28a? Rashi, Arama, and others refer דכּיו to דּכּים = נדכּאים (מדכּים). Thus also perhaps the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., which translates τοὺς ἐπιτριμμοὺς (not: ἐπιτετριμμένους) αὐτῆς. C. B. Michaelis: <hi type="italic">Lingua falsitatis odio habet contritos suos, h. e. eos quos falsitate ac mendacio laedit contritosque facit</hi>. Hitzig objects that it is more correct to say: <hi type="italic">conterit perosos sibi</hi>. And certainly this lay nearer, on which account Fleischer remarks: in 28a there is to be supposed a poetic transposition of the ideas (Hypallage): <hi type="italic">homo qui lingua ad calumnias abutitur conterit eos quos odit</hi>. The poet makes ישׂנא the main conception, because it does not come to him so readily to say that the lying tongue bruises those against whom it is directed, as that it is hatred, which is active in this. To say this was by no means superfluous. There are men who find pleasure in repeating and magnifying scandalously that which is depreciatory and disadvantageous to their neighbour unsubstantiated, without being at all conscious of any particular ill-will or personal enmity against him; but this proverb says that such untruthful tongue-thrashing proceeds always from a transgression of the commandment, “Thou shalt not hate thy brother,” <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev 19:17</reference>, and not merely from the want of love, but from a state of mind which is the direct opposite of love (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.10.18">Pro 10:18</reference>). Ewald finds it incongruous that 28a speaks of that which others have to suffer from the lying tongue, whereas the whole connection of this proverb requires that the tongue should here be regarded as bringing ruin upon its owner himself. But of the destruction which the wicked tongue prepares for others many proverbs also speak, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.13">Pro 12:13</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.4">Pro 17:4</reference>, לשׁון הוּת; and 28b does not mention that the smooth tongue (written וּפה־חלק with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>) brings injury upon itself (an idea which must be otherwise expressed; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.14.32">Pro 14:32</reference>), but that it brings injury and ruin on those who have pleasure in its flatteries (חלקות, <reference osisRef="Ps.12.3">Psa 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa 30:10</reference>), and are befooled thereby: <hi type="italic">os blandiloquum</hi> (<hi type="italic">blanditiis dolum tegens</hi>) <hi type="italic">ad casum impellit, sc. alios</hi> (Fleischer).  <chapter eID="Prov.26"/> <div eID="gen11742" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXVI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AS snow in summer, and as rain in harvest <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Unbecoming and unseasonable.</ns0:note>, so honour is not seemly for a fool <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Because he neither de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serves it, nor knows how to use it, but his folly is both increased and publickly manifested by it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 As the bird by wandring <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">From place to place, by its perpetual restlesness, it secures it self from the Fowler that he cannot shoot at it, nor spread his Net over it.</ns0:note>, as the swallow by fly<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, so the curse causless shall not come <ns0:hi>d.</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>f</ns0:hi> To wit, upon the innocent Person, but he shall escape from it like a Bird, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 32. 9. Ch. 10. 13<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> A whip for the horse, a bridle <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which was very proper and usual for an Ass, when they rode upon it, (as the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> most commonly did) though not to restrain him from running away, which is the principal use of it in Horses, yet that the Rider might rule and guide him, which was very ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary for that stupid Creature. Although the ancient Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters render it <ns0:hi>a Goad,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Spur,</ns0:hi> or somthing of the like Nature and use.</ns0:note> for the ass, and a rod <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which is most proper and necessary for him. Not words, but blows, must make him better.</ns0:note> for the fools back.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Answer not a fool <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">How can these contrary rules be reconciled, <ns0:hi>answer</ns0:hi> him <ns0:hi>not,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>answer</ns0:hi> him? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Easily, by considering the difference of Persons, and Times, and Places, and other circumstances, and of the manner of answering. And such seemingly contradictory Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepts are not onely used by, but are esteemed Elegant in, other Authors, <ns0:hi>Answer</ns0:hi> him <ns0:hi>not,</ns0:hi> when he is incorrigible, or when he is enflamed with Passion or Wine, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> or when it is not necessary, nor likely to do him good. <ns0:hi>Answer</ns0:hi> him, when he is capable of receiving good by it, or when it is necessary for the glory of God, or for the discharge of a Man's duty, or for the good of others.</ns0:note> according to his folly <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">So as to imitate his folly, by such passionate, or reproachful, or foolish speeches as he useth to thee.</ns0:note>, lest thou also be like unto him <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Shew thy self to be as great a fool as he.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Answer a fool according to his folly <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">So as his folly needs and requires, convincing him strongly, reproving him sharply, exposing him to just shame, and correct<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing him with a Rod, when he deserves it, and thou hast a just power to use it.</ns0:note>, lest he be wise in <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> his own eyes.</ns0:note> his own conceit <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Lest thy silence make him arrogant and pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sumptuous, as if his words were unanswerable.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">He that employeth a Fool upon any important Errant or Busi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness which is too hard for him.</ns0:note>, cutteth off the feet <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, of his Messenger, he bids one go that wants Legs, he sends one who wants that discreti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, which is as necessary for that employment as Legs are for going.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> drinketh <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> violen<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> damage <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He bringeth upon himself abundance of loss and mischief, not onely spoiling that business about which he sends him, but making himself contemptible to the Person to whom he sends him, and to others with him, as if he had not common prudence to chuse a fit Messenger, and giving occasion by the folly of his Messenger to further misunderstandings, and jealousies, and inconveniences. For the Phrase, we may observe that <ns0:hi>drinking</ns0:hi> in Scripture fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently notes the plentiful doing or receiving of any thing, as they who multiply sins are said to <ns0:hi>drink Iniquity like Water, Iob</ns0:hi> 15. 16. & 34. 7. and they who are greatly afflicted are commonly said to <ns0:hi>drink the Cup.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:538" />7 The legs of the lame <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> are lift<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed up.</ns0:note> are not equal <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Heb. As (which note of similitude is plainly understood from the particle, <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> in the following clause) <ns0:hi>the legs of the lame are lifted up,</ns0:hi> to wit, in going, or rather in dancing, which is done with great inequality and uncomeliness.</ns0:note>, so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rable in the mouth of fools <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">No less absurd and inde<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cent are wise and pious speeches from a foolish and ungodly man, whose actions grosly contradict them, whereby he makes them contemptible, and himself ridiculous.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>As he that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> a</ns0:hi> precious <ns0:hi>stone in an heap of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> As he that bindeth a stone in a sling <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Whereby he hinders his own design of throwing the stone out of it. Or, who fastens it there only for a season, that he may speedily and violently throw it away. Or, as it is rendred in our margent, and by many others, <ns0:hi>As he that putteth</ns0:hi> a precious <ns0:hi>stone</ns0:hi> (Heb. <ns0:hi>a stone,</ns0:hi> which is oft emphatically used for a precious stone, both in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 39. 10. 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 29. 8. and elsewhere, and also in other Authors) <ns0:hi>in an heap of stones,</ns0:hi> where it is obscured and lost.</ns0:note>, so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he that giveth honour to a fool <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">No less absurd is he that giveth to a Fool that Honour and Praise which he is not capable either of receiving, or retaining, or using aright, but it is quite wasted upon him, and doth him more hurt than good.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">As a thorn is in a Drunkards hand, which he cannot hold and manage cautiously, but employeth to his own and others hurt.</ns0:note>, so <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">As improper and unprofitable, and, by accident, hurtful to him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self and others. See on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a parable in the mouth of fools.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>a great</ns0:hi> man <ns0:hi>grieveth all, he hireth the fool, he hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reth also trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gressors.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> The great <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> that formed all <ns0:hi>things,</ns0:hi> both re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wardeth the fool, and rewardeth transgressors <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">God, who is oft called <ns0:hi>great,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 86. 10. & 135. 5. &c. and is described by the name of <ns0:hi>the most high,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Ps.</ns0:hi> 9. 2. & 21. 7. &c. who created all things, and therefore observeth and governeth all men and things, will certainly give that recompence which is meet for, and deserved by <ns0:hi>Fools and Transgressors, i. e.</ns0:hi> by such as sin either through ignorance and heedlesness, or wilfully and wickedly. Or, as it is in the margent, <ns0:hi>A great</ns0:hi> man (A Prince or Potentate, who are called by this title, <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 1. 8. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 1. 3. &c.) <ns0:hi>grieveth</ns0:hi> (as this word is used, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 51. 9. & 53. 5. and elsewhere) <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> (to wit, all that are subject to him, or all that stand in his way) <ns0:hi>he hireth</ns0:hi> (as this word most commonly signifies) <ns0:hi>the fools, he hireth al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so transgressors.</ns0:hi> So the sense is It is the manner of many Princes to vex and oppress their Subjects, which because they cannot do by themselves alone, they hire others, both <ns0:hi>fools,</ns0:hi> who do not know or consider what they do, and <ns0:hi>transgressors,</ns0:hi> who are ready to exe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cute all their commands, right or wrong, that they may be their instruments in that work.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
